nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For each~$a$, we write the eigendecomposition of $A_a$ as follows: \begin{equation*} A_a = \sum_i \lambda_{a, i} \cdot\ket{u_{a, i}} \bra{u_{a, i}}. \end{equation*} Let \begin{equation} 0 < \delta \leq 1/2 \end{equation} be a number to be decided later. Let $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta:[0, 1] \rightarrow \{0, 1\}$ be the truncation function defined as \begin{equation*} \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{rl} 1 & \text{if } x \geq 1- \delta,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} Then for each~$a$ we define the matrix $R_a$ \begin{equation*} R_a = \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a) = \sum_i \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(\lambda_{a, i}) \cdot \ket{u_{a, i}} \bra{u_{a, i}}. \end{equation*} To analyze this, we will require the following technical lemma. \begin{lemma} For any $x \in [0, 1]$, \begin{equation*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} This is proved by case analysis. First, suppose that $x \geq 1 - \delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 1$. In addition, because $\delta \leq 1/2$ by \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}, $ x \geq 1 - \delta \geq 1/2 \geq \delta. $ Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = (1-x)^2\\ &\leq (1-x)\\ &\leq (1-x) \cdot \frac{x}{\delta} \tag{because $x \geq \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} Next, suppose that $x < 1 -\delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 0$. Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = x^2\\ &\leq x\\ &\leq x \cdot \frac{(1-x)}{\delta} \tag{because $x \leq 1- \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} This concludes the proof. \end{proof} As a result, for each~$a$, \Cref{lem:trunc-inequality} implies that \begin{equation*} (A_a - R_a)^2 = (A_a - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (A_a - (A_a)^2). \end{equation*} Thus, \begin{align*} \sum_a \Vert (A_a - R_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Vert^2 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - R_a)^2 \otimes I\ket{\psi} &\leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - (A_a)^2) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &\leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot 2\zeta. \tag{by \Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}} \end{align*} This implies that $A_a \otimes I \approx_{2\zeta/\delta} R_a \otimes I$. Next, for each $x \in [0, 1]$, it follows from the definition of $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta$ that \begin{equation*} \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot x. \end{equation*} Thus, for each~$a$ \begin{equation*} R_a = \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a) \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot A_a. \end{equation*} Summing over all~$a$, \begin{equation*} R = \sum_a R_a \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot \sum_a A_a = \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot A = \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot I, \end{equation*} because~$A$ is a measurement. We note that \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{1-\delta} = \frac{1}{1-\delta} \cdot \frac{1 + 2\delta}{1 + 2\delta} = \frac{1 + 2\delta}{1 + \delta - 2\delta^2} \leq 1 + 2\delta, \end{equation*} because \begin{equation*} 1 + \delta - 2\delta^2 = 1 + \delta\cdot(1-2\delta)\geq 1 \end{equation*} when $\delta \leq 1/2$, which we assumed in \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}. Hence, \begin{equation*} R \leq (1+ 2\delta) \cdot I. \end{equation*} The lemma now follows by setting $\delta = \sqrt{\zeta}$. Note that we required that $\delta$ be at most $1/2$, which follows from our assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}.
nodes.statement_short: Truncate eigenvalues of A_a at threshold 1-delta, bound the error by the near-projectivity of A, and bound R by (1+2delta)I; set delta=sqrt(zeta).

nodes.name: Equation (21)
nodes.statement: 0 < \delta \leq 1/2
nodes.label: eq:bound-on-delta

nodes.name: Truncation inequality
nodes.statement: For any $x \in [0, 1]$, \begin{equation*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{equation*}
assumptions: For any $x \in [0, 1]$,
nodes.label: lem:trunc-inequality

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is proved by case analysis. First, suppose that $x \geq 1 - \delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 1$. In addition, because $\delta \leq 1/2$ by \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}, $ x \geq 1 - \delta \geq 1/2 \geq \delta. $ Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = (1-x)^2\\ &\leq (1-x)\\ &\leq (1-x) \cdot \frac{x}{\delta} \tag{because $x \geq \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} Next, suppose that $x < 1 -\delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 0$. Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = x^2\\ &\leq x\\ &\leq x \cdot \frac{(1-x)}{\delta} \tag{because $x \leq 1- \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether x is above the truncation threshold.

nodes.name: Rank reduction
nodes.statement: There exists a set of projection matrices $\{Q_a\}$ such that \begin{equation*} A_a \otimes I \approx_{12\sqrt{\zeta}} Q_a \otimes I. \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} Q:= \sum_a Q_a \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I. \end{equation*} Furthermore, $Q$ has bounded total rank: \begin{equation*} \sum_a \mathrm{rank}(Q_a) \leq d. \end{equation*}
conclusions: There exists a set of projection matrices $\{Q_a\}$ such that
nodes.label: lem:projective-low-rank-sum

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Keep only the d basis vectors of the R_a ranges with largest overlap with psi; the discarded ones carry total overlap at most 4sqrt(zeta).

nodes.name: Equation (22)
nodes.statement: r = \sum_{a} r_a = \sum_{a} \mathrm{tr}(R_a) = \mathrm{tr}(R) \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \mathrm{tr}(I) = (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot d.
nodes.label: eq:bound-on-r

nodes.name: Equation (23)
nodes.label: eq:total-overlap

nodes.name: Equation (24)
nodes.statement: |\mathsf{Small}| = r - |\mathsf{Large}| = r - d \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot d - d = 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot d \leq 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot r.
nodes.label: eq:size-of-small-is-small

nodes.name: Equation (25)
nodes.statement: \sum_{(a, i) \in \mathsf{Small}} o_{a, i} \leq \frac{|\mathsf{Small}|}{r} \sum_{a, i} o_{a,i} &\leq 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot \sum_{a, i} o_{a,i} \tag{by \Cref{eq:size-of-small-is-small}}\\ &\leq 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \tag{by \Cref{eq:total-overlap}}\\ & \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta},
nodes.label: eq:small-overlaps

nodes.name: Completeness of Q
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:Q-completeness

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: To begin, we claim that \begin{align} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{because the $Q_a$'s are projective}\\ & \approx_{5 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{align} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \otimes I) \cdot ((Q_a - A_a) \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~&\sqrt{\sum_a\bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{1+2\sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot \sqrt{12\sqrt{\zeta}} \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{12\sqrt{\zeta}}, \end{align*} where the last line uses the assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}. Next, we claim that \begin{equation} \eqref{eq:Q-for-an-A} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{4 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((Q_a - A_a) \otimes I) \cdot (A_a \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~&\sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a\bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{12 \sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot 1. \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}} \end{align*} In conclusion, \begin{align*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 9 \zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:Q-for-an-A,eq:another-Q-for-A}}\\ & \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 2\zeta - 9\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}}\\ & \geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 11 \zeta^{1/4} \nonumber\\ & = 1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Swap Q_a for A_a twice inside the squared weight using Cauchy-Schwarz, then use near-projectivity of A.

nodes.name: Equation (28)
nodes.statement: \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{because the $Q_a$'s are projective}\\ & \approx_{5 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}.
nodes.label: eq:Q-for-an-A

nodes.name: Equation (30)
nodes.statement: \eqref{eq:Q-for-an-A} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{4 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}.
nodes.label: eq:another-Q-for-A

nodes.name: Completeness of sqrt(Q)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 1 - 12 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:sqrt-Q-completeness

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $Q = \sum_i 
u_i \ket{u_i}  ra{u_i}$ be the eigendecomposition of~$Q$. Then because $Q \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I$, each eigenvalue $
u_i$ is at most $1+2\sqrt{\zeta}$. Thus,  egin{equation*} \sqrt{Q} = \sum_i \sqrt{
u_i} \ket{u_i} ra{u_i} \geq  rac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}}} \cdot \sum_i 
u_i \ket{u_i} ra{u_i} =  rac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}}} \cdot Q. \end{equation*} We note that  egin{equation*}  rac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}}} \geq  rac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta} + \zeta}} =  rac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\zeta}} =  rac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot \Big( rac{1-\sqrt{\zeta}}{1-\sqrt{\zeta}}\Big) =  rac{1-\sqrt{\zeta}}{1 - \zeta} \geq 1 - \sqrt{\zeta}. \end{equation*} Hence, $\sqrt{Q} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot Q$. As a result, \Cref{lem:Q-completeness} implies that  egin{equation*}  ra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot ra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \left(1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}ight) \geq 1 -\sqrt{\zeta} - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*} This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound sqrt(Q) >= (1-sqrt(zeta))Q using the eigenvalue bound on Q, then apply completeness of Q.

nodes.name: Q is almost projective
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \sum_a (Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a) \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot I. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:q-almost-projective

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum} implies that $Q \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I$. As a result, \begin{align*} &\sum_a Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - \sum_a Q_a\\ \leq ~&(1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \sum_a Q_a \cdot I \cdot Q_a - \sum_a Q_a \\ = ~&(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \sum_a Q_a - \sum_a Q_a \tag{because the $Q_a$'s are projectors}\\ = ~&(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot Q - Q\\ = ~& 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot Q\\ \leq~& 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I\\ \leq~& 2 \sqrt{\zeta} \cdot 2 \cdot I. \tag{by \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}} \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound Q by (1+2sqrt(zeta))I and use that each Q_a is a projector.

nodes.name: Matrix decomposition of Q_a
nodes.statement: For each $a$, let $m_a$ be the rank of $Q_a$. Let $\ket{v_{a, 1}}, \ldots, \ket{v_{a, m_a}}$ be an orthonormal basis for the range of $Q_a$, so that \begin{equation*} Q_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}. \end{equation*} Let $m = \sum_a m_a$, and consider an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^m$ consisting of vectors $\ket{a, i}$ for each $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$. For each $a$, define the matrix \begin{equation*} X_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{v_{a, i}}. \end{equation*} In addition, define the matrix \begin{equation} X = \sum_a X_a = \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{v_{a, i}}. \end{equation} Finally, we let $T = \{T_a\}$ be the projective measurement on $\mathbb C^m$ defined as \begin{equation*} T_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i}\bra{a, i}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write each Q_a via an orthonormal basis of its range, define X_a mapping it to basis vectors |a,i>, X = sum_a X_a, and the projective measurement T.

nodes.name: Equation (31)
nodes.statement: X = \sum_a X_a = \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{v_{a, i}}.
nodes.label: eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition

nodes.name: X_a equals T_a X
nodes.statement: For each~$a$, $\displaystyle X_a = T_a \cdot X. $
nodes.label: lem:xa-t

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is a simple calculation: \begin{equation*} T_a \cdot X = \Big(\sum_i^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{a,i}\Big)\cdot \Big( \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i}\bra{v_{a, i}}\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i}\bra{v_{a, i}} = X_a.\qedhere \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Q_a restated
nodes.statement: For each~$a$, \begin{equation*} Q_a = X^\dagger_a \cdot X_a = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X. \end{equation*}
conclusions: Q_a = X^\dagger_a \cdot X_a = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X.
nodes.label: lem:qa-restated

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The first equality follows from \begin{align*} X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a &= \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{a, i} \Big) \cdot \Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, j}}\bra{a, j} \Big)^\dagger\nonumber\\ &= \sum_{i, j=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{a, i} \cdot \ket{a, j} \bra{v_{a, j}} = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}} = Q_a. \end{align*} The remaining equalities follow from \Cref{lem:xa-t} and the fact that~$T$ is a projective measurement. \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = (X^\dagger \cdot T_a) \cdot (T_a \cdot X) = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X.\qedhere \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute X_a^dagger X_a directly; the other equalities follow from X_a = T_a X and projectivity of T.

nodes.name: SVD of X
nodes.statement: Let $X = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger$ be the singular value decomposition (SVD) of~$X$. Because~$X$ is an $m \times d$ matrix, the definition of the SVD states that $U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary matrix, $V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary matrix, and $\Sigma_{m\times d}$ is an $m \times d$ diagonal matrix with nonnegative real numbers on its diagonal.

nodes.name: Rectangular identity and singular value matrices
nodes.statement: For positive integers $h$ and~$w$, we will write $I_{h \times w}$ for the $h \times w$ matrix with $1$'s on its diagonal and $0$'s everywhere else. For integers $h, w \geq m$, we also write $\Sigma_{h \times w}$ for the $h \times w$ diagonal matrix whose diagonal agrees with $\Sigma_{m \times d}$'s; namely, $(\Sigma_{h \times w})_{i, i} = (\Sigma_{m \times d})_{i,i}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$ and $(\Sigma_{h \times w})_{i, i} = 0$ for all $i > m$. We note that because $\Sigma_{m \times d}$ is a real-valued diagonal matrix, $(\Sigma_{h \times w})^\dagger = \Sigma_{w \times h}$.

nodes.name: X squared
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} X \cdot X^\dagger = U \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger, \quad \text{and} \quad X^\dagger \cdot X = Q = V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger. \end{equation*}
conclusions: X^\dagger \cdot X = Q = V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger.
nodes.label: lem:X-squared

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First, \begin{align*} X \cdot X^\dagger &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}. \end{align*} Second, \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot X & = \sum_a X^\dagger \cdot T_a X \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ &= \sum_a Q_a \tag{by \Cref{lem:qa-restated}}\\ &= Q. \end{align*} In addition, we can rewrite $X^\dagger \cdot X$ as \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot X &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\ &= V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger. \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation using the SVD and the restated form of Q_a.

nodes.name: X expression equals Q expression
nodes.statement: For each~$a$, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a = Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a. \end{equation*}
conclusions: X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a = Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a.
nodes.label: lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Using~\Cref{lem:X-squared} and~\Cref{lem:qa-restated}, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot Q \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a. \end{equation*} Similarly, because $Q_a$ is projective, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a = (X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot (X^\dagger \cdot X_a) = Q_a \cdot Q_a = Q_a. \end{equation*} Finally, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a. \end{equation*} Putting these together, \begin{align*} &X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a\\ =~& X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger - 2 \cdot X\cdot X^\dagger + I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a\\ =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - 2 \cdot Q_a + Q_a\\ =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a. \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square and evaluate each term with the X-squared and Q_a-restated lemmas.

nodes.name: Intuition: SVD when Q is a projective measurement
nodes.statement: Suppose that the $Q_a$'s actually formed a projective measurement. This would imply that the vectors $\ket{v_{a, i}}$, over all $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$ form an orthonormal set. Then the SVD would actually have already been provided in \Cref{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition}; for each $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$, the corresponding singular value would be~$1$ and the corresponding left- and right-singular vectors would be $\ket{a, i}$ and $\ket{v_{a, i}}$, respectively. In particular, we would have $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$ and $X = U \cdot I_{m \times d}\cdot V^\dagger$.
nodes.statement_short: If the Q_a formed a projective measurement, X would already be in SVD form with all singular values 1.

nodes.name: Definition of P
nodes.statement: Define the matrix \begin{equation*} \widehat{X} = U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger. \end{equation*} In addition, for each $a$, define the matrices \begin{equation*} \widehat{X}_a = T_a \cdot \widehat{X}, \quad P_a = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Replace the singular values of X by 1 to get X-hat, and set P_a = X-hat_a^dagger X-hat_a.

nodes.name: P_a restated
nodes.statement: For each~$a$, \begin{equation*} P_a = \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:pa-restated

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This follows from the definition of $\widehat{X}^\dagger_a$ and the fact that $T$ is a projective measurement: \begin{equation*} P_a = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a = (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a) \cdot (T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) = \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}.\qedhere \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Follows from the definition and projectivity of T.

nodes.name: X-hat squared
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = I_{m \times m}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:X-hat-squared

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First, \begin{align*} \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger &= (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}\\ &= I_{m \times m}, \end{align*} where the last step uses the fact that~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation from the SVD factors.

nodes.name: X times X-hat
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger, \quad \text{and} \quad X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} = \sqrt{Q}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:X-times-X-hat

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First, \begin{align*} X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}. \end{align*} Second, \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= \sqrt{V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger}\\ &= \sqrt{Q}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}} \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation from the SVD factors.

nodes.name: Squared difference
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \leq (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:squared-difference

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By~\Cref{lem:X-squared,lem:X-hat-squared,lem:X-times-X-hat}, \begin{align*} (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger & = X \cdot X^\dagger - X\cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger - \widehat{X} \cdot X^\dagger + \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger\\ & = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - 2 \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger+ I_{m \times m}\\ & = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 - 2 \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m} \right) \cdot U^\dagger\\ & = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger. \end{align*} Because $\Sigma_{m \times m}$ and $I_{m \times m}$ are commuting, \begin{equation*} (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2 \leq (\Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2 = (\Sigma_{m\times m}^2 - I_{m \times m})^2. \end{equation*} As a result, \begin{align*} U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger & \leq U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger\\ & = \left(U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - I_{m \times m} \right)^2\\ &= (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}} \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Write both sides in the U basis and compare (Sigma-I)^2 with (Sigma^2-I)^2 entrywise.

nodes.name: Projectivity of P
nodes.statement: $P = \{P_a\}$ forms a projective sub-measurement.
nodes.label: lem:P-projectivity

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $a, b$ be (possibly distinct) outcomes. Then \begin{align*} P_a \cdot P_b &= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \cdot (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X}) \tag{by \Cref{lem:pa-restated}}\\ &= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X}) \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\ &= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \cdot \boldsymbol{1}[a = b] \tag{because~$T$ is a projective measurement}\\ &= P_a \cdot \boldsymbol{1}[a=b]. \tag{by \Cref{lem:pa-restated}} \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Compute P_a P_b using X-hat X-hat^dagger = I and projectivity of T.

nodes.name: P is close to Q
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} Q_a \otimes I \approx_{30\zeta^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:P-Q-approx

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Our goal is to upper-bound the quantity \begin{align} &\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \bra{\psi} P\otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}, \end{align} where the last step uses the projectivity of~$Q$ and~$P$. We bound the four terms in \Cref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} separately. First, by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}, \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 1+2\sqrt{\zeta}. \end{equation*} Second, because~$P$ is a sub-measurement, \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} P \otimes I\ket{\psi} \leq 1. \end{equation*} The third term and fourth terms are significantly more complicated to bound. As they are complex conjugates of each other, we can write their sum as \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = 2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big). \end{equation} We now focus on the expression on the right-hand side of \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates}. To begin, we use \Cref{lem:qa-restated} to rewrite it as \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*} The main step will be to show that we can exchange the second $X$ for an $\widehat{X}$, i.e. \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{multline*} \Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X})) \otimes I) \cdot(P_a \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}. \end{multline*} The expression inside the first square root is \begin{align*} & \sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ \leq~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:squared-difference}}\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}}\\ \leq~& 4\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by~\Cref{lem:q-almost-projective}}\\ =~& 4\sqrt{\zeta}. \end{align*} The expression inside the second square root is at most~$1$ because~$P$ is a sub-measurement. Next, we claim that the \Cref{eq:add-a-hat} is in fact a real-valued expression. To see this, \begin{align*} \eqref{eq:add-a-hat} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:xa-t,lem:pa-restated}}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ &= \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-times-X-hat}}, \end{align*} which is real-valued because~$Q$ is positive semidefinite. As a result, we have \begin{align*} \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) & \geq \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) - 2\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:add-a-hat}}\\ & = \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi}- 2\zeta^{1/4}\\ & \geq (1 - 12 \zeta^{1/4}) - 2\zeta^{1/4}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:sqrt-Q-completeness}} \end{align*} In total, \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates} shows that \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 2 \cdot(1 - 14\zeta^{1/4}). \end{equation*} Putting everything together, we conclude that \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) + 1 - 2\cdot (1-14\zeta^{1/4}) = 2\sqrt{\zeta} + 28 \zeta^{1/4} \leq 30 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the squared distance into four terms; the cross terms are handled by exchanging X for X-hat, which costs 2zeta^{1/4} via the squared-difference lemma, leaving <sqrt(Q)>.

nodes.name: Equation (32)
nodes.statement: &\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \bra{\psi} P\otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi},
nodes.label: eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound

nodes.name: Equation (33)
nodes.statement: \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = 2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big).
nodes.label: eq:complex-conjugates

nodes.name: Equation (34)
nodes.statement: \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}.
nodes.label: eq:add-a-hat

nodes.name: Main induction
nodes.statement: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test. Let $k \geq md$ be an integer. Then there exists a measurement $G \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ such that on average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^{m}$, \begin{equation*} A^{u}_a \otimes I \simeq_{\sigma} I \otimes G_{[g(u)=a]}, \end{equation*} where $\sigma = m^2 \cdot \bigl(\nu + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\bigr)$ and $\nu = 1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + \delta^{1/1024} + \gamma^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\big)$.
nodes.statement_short: A good symmetric strategy admits a measurement over individual-degree-d polynomials sigma-consistent with the points measurement, sigma = m^2(nu + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}).
assumptions: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test.
Let $k \geq md$ be an integer.
conclusions: Then there exists a measurement $G \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ such that on average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^{m}$,
nodes.label: thm:main-induction

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Suppose $(\psi, A^{\mathrm{A}},B^{\mathrm{A}},L^{\mathrm{A}},A^{\mathrm{B}},B^{\mathrm{B}},L^{\mathrm{B}})$ is a (not necessarily symmetric) strategy which passes the $(m, q, d)$-low individual degree test with probability $(1-\epsilon)$. Throughout this proof we will refer to this as the \emph{original strategy}. Then because each of the three subtests occurs with probability $1/3$, $(\psi, A^{\mathrm{A}},B^{\mathrm{A}},L^{\mathrm{A}},A^{\mathrm{B}},B^{\mathrm{B}},L^{\mathrm{B}})$ is a $(3\epsilon, 3\epsilon, 3\epsilon)$-good strategy. We now would like to apply \Cref{thm:main-induction}, but it only applies to strategies which are symmetric. So we will apply a standard construction to ``symmetrize'' our strategy, apply \Cref{thm:main-induction}, and then ``unsymmetrize'' the resulting $\{G_g\}$ measurement to obtain $\{G^{\mathrm{A}}_g\}$ and $\{G^{\mathrm{B}}_g\}$ measurements. For simplicity, we will assume that Player~$\mathrm{A}$ and~$\mathrm{B}$'s Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{B}}$ are both $\mathbb C^d$, for some~$d$. (This argument can be extended to the case of different dimensions in a straightforward manner.) We will introduce two additional registers, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}'} =\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{B'}} = \mathbb C^2$, referred to as the \emph{role registers}. Then the symmetrized state is given by  egin{equation*} \ket{\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}} = \ket{0}_{\mathrm{A}'}\ket{1}_{\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\psi}_{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}} +\ket{1}_{\mathrm{A}'}\ket{0}_{\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\psi_{\mathrm{swap}}}_{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}} \in (\mathbb C^2_{\mathrm{A}'} \otimes \mathbb C^d_{\mathrm{A}}) \otimes (\mathbb C^2_{\mathrm{B}'} \otimes \mathbb C^d_{\mathrm{B}}), \end{equation*} where $\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{swap}}}$ denotes $\ket{\psi}$ with its two registers swapped. Note that the resulting state $\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}}$ is symmetric under the exchange of its two registers. Next, we define the symmetrized measurement $A_{\mathrm{sym}} = \{(A_{\mathrm{sym}})^u_a\}$ as follows  egin{equation*} (A_{\mathrm{sym}})^u_a = \ket{0} ra{0} \otimes A^{\mathrm{A},u}_a + \ket{1}  ra{1} \otimes A^{\mathrm{B},u}_a, \end{equation*} and we define $B_{\mathrm{sym}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ similarly. The strategy $(\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}, A_{\mathrm{sym}}, B_{\mathrm{sym}}, L_{\mathrm{sym}})$ is symmetric; we refer to it as the \emph{symmetrized strategy}. It has the following interpretation: the two players measure their respective role registers in the standard basis; the one that receives a ``$0$'' will act as Player~A in the original strategy, and the one that receives a ``$1$'' will act as Player~B in the original strategy. As a result, the symmetrized strategy is also a $(3\epsilon, 3\epsilon, 3\epsilon)$-good strategy. Now we apply \cref{thm:main-induction} to the symmetrized strategy. To do so, set  egin{align*} &1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\Big((3\epsilon)^{1/1024} + (3\epsilon)^{1/1024} + (3\epsilon)^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big)\ \leq{}& 10000 k^2 m^2 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big) =:

We have now derived everything we wanted, except that~$G$ is not necessarily projective. To remedy this, we apply the orthogonalization lemma for measurements (\Cref{lem:orthonormalization-main-lemma}) to \Cref{eq:G-self-consistency}. It implies the existence of two projective sub-measurements $P^{\mathrm{A}} = \{P^{\mathrm{A}}\}, P^{\mathrm{B}} = \{P^{\mathrm{B}}\} \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$ such that  egin{align*} G^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I &\approx_{100\zeta_1^{1/4}} P^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I,\ I \otimes G^{\mathrm{B}}_g &\approx_{100\zeta_1^{1/4}} I \otimes P^{\mathrm{B}}_g. \end{align*} Hence, \Cref{prop:completing-to-measurement} implies that we can complete $P^{\mathrm{A}}$ and~$P^{\mathrm{B}}$ to projective measurements $Q^{\mathrm{A}} = \{Q^{\mathrm{A}}\}, Q^{\mathrm{B}} = \{Q^{\mathrm{B}}\} \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ such that  egin{align} G^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I &\approx_{\zeta_2} Q^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I,\ I \otimes G^{\mathrm{B}}_g &\approx_{\zeta_2} I \otimes Q^{\mathrm{B}}_g.

Because both of these measurements are projective, \Cref{prop:simeq-to-approx} then implies that  egin{equation} Q_g^{\mathrm{A}} \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta_3/2} I \otimes Q_g^{\mathrm{B}}, \end{equation} By the data processing inequality (\Cref{prop:simeq-data-processing}),  egin{equation} Q_{[g(u)=a]}^{\mathrm{A}} \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta_3/2} I \otimes Q_{[g(u)=a]}^{\mathrm{B}}, \end{equation} Next, \Cref{prop:triangle-sub}, applied to \Cref{eq:G-self-consistency} and \Cref{eq:G-with-Q-A} implies that  egin{equation*} Q^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta_1} I \otimes G^{\mathrm{B}}_g. \end{equation*} By data processing (\Cref{prop:simeq-data-processing}),  egin{equation} Q^{\mathrm{A}}_{[g(u)=a]} \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta_1} I \otimes G^{\mathrm{B}}_{[g(u)=a]}. \end{equation} Now we apply the triangle inequality (\Cref{prop:simeq-triangle-inequality}) to \Cref{eq:cons-b,eq:ok-almost-there-ok,eq:just-data-processed-the-heck-outta-this}, which implies that  egin{equation} A^{\mathrm{A},u}_a \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta_4} I \otimes Q^{\mathrm{B}}_{[g(u)=a]}, \end{equation} where $\zeta_4 = 2\sigma + 2 \sqrt{\zeta_1 + \zeta_3/2}$. First,  egin{align*} \sigma &= m^2\cdot\left(10000 k^2 m^2 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big) + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}ight)\ &\leq 10000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024} + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\Big). \end{align*} Next, using $10000^{1/2} = 100$,  egin{align*} \zeta_1 &= 2\sigma + 2\sqrt{3\epsilon + 2\sigma} + md/q\ & \leq 2\cdot\Big(10000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024} + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \qquad\qquad+ 2\cdot \Big( 3 \epsilon + 10000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024} + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\Big)\Big)^{1/2} + md/q\ & \leq 2\cdot\Big(10000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024} + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \qquad\qquad+ 2\cdot \Big( 2 \epsilon^{1/2} + 100 k m^2 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/2048} + (d/q)^{1/2048} + e^{-k/(160000m^2)}\Big)\Big) + md/q\ & \leq 20204 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/2048} + (d/q)^{1/2048} + e^{-k/(160000m^2)}\Big). \end{align*} Next, using the fact that $20204^{1/4} \leq 12$ and $20204^{1/8} \leq 4$,  egin{align*} \zeta_2 &= 200\zeta_1^{1/4} + 40\zeta_1^{1/8}\ & \leq 200 \Big(20204 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/2048} + (d/q)^{1/2048} + e^{-k/(160000m^2)}\Big)\Big)^{1/4}\ & \qquad\qquad+ 40 \Big(20204 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/2048} + (d/q)^{1/2048} + e^{-k/(160000m^2)}\Big)\Big)^{1/8}\ & \leq 200 \Big(12 k m \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/8192} + (d/q)^{1/8192} + e^{-k/(640000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \qquad\qquad+ 40 \Big(4 k m \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/16384} + (d/q)^{1/16384} + e^{-k/(1280000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \leq 2560 km \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/16384} + (d/q)^{1/16384} + e^{-k/(1280000m^2)}\Big). \end{align*} Next, using $6\cdot 20204 + 6 \cdot 2560 \leq 150000$,  egin{equation*} \zeta_3 = 6 \zeta_1 + 6 \zeta_2 \leq 150000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/16384} + (d/q)^{1/16384} + e^{-k/(1280000m^2)}\Big). \end{equation*} Next, using $\sqrt{20204} \leq 143$, $\sqrt{150000} \leq 388$, and $2 \cdot (10000+143+388) \leq 40000$,  egin{align*} \zeta_4 &= 2\sigma + 2 \sqrt{\zeta_1 + \zeta_3/2}\ & \leq 2 \cdot \Big(10000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024} + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \qquad \qquad + 2 \cdot \Big(20204 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/2048} + (d/q)^{1/2048} + e^{-k/(160000m^2)}\Big) \ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad+ 150000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/16384} + (d/q)^{1/16384} + e^{-k/(1280000m^2)}\Big)\Big)^{1/2}\ & \leq 2 \cdot \Big(10000 k^2 m^4 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024} + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \qquad \qquad + 2 \cdot \Big(143 k m^2 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/4096} + (d/q)^{1/4096} + e^{-k/(320000m^2)}\Big) \ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad+ 388 k m^2 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/32768} + (d/q)^{1/32768} + e^{-k/(2560000m^2)}\Big)\Big)\ & \leq 40000k^2m^4 \cdot\Big(\epsilon^{1/32768} + (d/q)^{1/32768} + e^{-k/(2560000m^2)}\Big)\Big). \end{align*} Both this and $\zeta_3/2$ are less than  egin{equation*} 100000k^2m^4 \cdot\Big(\epsilon^{1/40000} + (d/q)^{1/40000} + e^{-k/(2560000m^2)}\Big)\Big). \end{equation*} Hence, \Cref{eq:one-goal,eq:another-goal,eq:third-goal} provide the three bounds we want. nodes.name: Self-improvement
nodes.statement: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test. Let $G \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$ be a sub-measurement with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item (Consistency with~$A$): On average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^{m}$, \begin{equation*} A^{u}_a \otimes I \simeq_{\nu} I \otimes G_{[g(u)=a]}. \end{equation*} \end{enumerate} Let \begin{equation*} \zeta = 3000m\cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/32} + \delta^{1/32} + (d/q)^{1/32}\Big). \end{equation*} Then there exists a projective sub-measurement $H \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item(Completeness): If $H = \sum_h H_h$, then \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} H \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\nu)-\zeta. \end{equation*} \item(Consistency with~$A$): On average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$, \begin{equation*} A^u_a \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta} I \otimes H_{[h(u) = a]}. \end{equation*} \item(Strong self-consistency): \begin{equation*} H_h \otimes I \approx_{\zeta} I \otimes H_h. \end{equation*} \item(Boundedness): There exists a positive-semidefinite matrix~$Z$ such that \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Z \otimes (I - H) \ket{\psi} \leq \zeta \end{equation*} and for each $h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, \begin{equation*} Z \geq \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}_{h(\boldsymbol{u})}\right). \end{equation*} \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Pasting
nodes.statement: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m+1,q,d)$ low individual degree test. Let $\{G^x\}_{x \in \mathbb F_q}$ denote a set of projective sub-measurements in $\polysub{m}{q}{d}$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item (Completeness): If $G = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_g G^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_g$, then \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} G \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 1 - \kappa. \end{equation*} \item (Consistency with~$A$): On average over $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}) \sim \mathbb F_q^{m+1}$, \begin{equation*} A^{u, x}_a \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta} I \otimes G^x_{[g(u)=a]}. \end{equation*} \item (Strong self-consistency): On average over~${\boldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q$, \begin{equation*} G^x_g \otimes I \approx_{\zeta} I \otimes G^x_g. \end{equation*} \item (Boundedness): There exists a positive-semidefinite matrix $Z^x$ for each $x \in \mathbb F_q$ such that \begin{equation*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \bra{\psi} (I-G^{{\boldsymbol{x}}})\otimes Z^{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \ket{\psi} \leq \zeta \end{equation*} and for each $x \in \mathbb F_q$ and $g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, \begin{equation*} Z^x \geq \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} A^{\boldsymbol{u}, x}_{g(\boldsymbol{u})}\right). \end{equation*} \end{enumerate} Let $k \geq 400md$ be an integer. Let \begin{align*} \nu &= 100 k^2m \cdot \left(\epsilon^{1/32} + \delta^{1/32} + \gamma^{1/32} + \zeta^{1/32} + (d/q)^{1/32}\right),\\ \sigma& = \kappa \cdot \left(1 + \frac{1}{100m}\right) + 2\nu + e^{- k/(80000m^2)}. \end{align*} Then there exists a ``pasted" measurement $H \in \polymeas{m+1}{q}{d}$ which satisfies the following property. \begin{enumerate} \item (Consistency with~$A$): On average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^{m+1}$, \begin{equation*} A^{u}_a \otimes I \simeq_{\sigma} I \otimes H_{[h(u)=a]}. \end{equation*} \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Appending a coordinate to lines and functions
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathbb F_q$. For each line $\ell \in \mathbb F_q^m$, we define $\mathrm{append}_x(\ell)$ to be the line in $\mathbb F_q^{m+1}$ containing every point $(u, x)$ such that $u \in \ell$. In addition, for each function $f : \ell \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$, we define $\mathrm{append}_x(f) : \mathrm{append}_x(\ell) \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$ such that for each $(u, x) \in \mathrm{append}_x(\ell)$, $\mathrm{append}_x(f)(u, x) = f(u)$.

nodes.name: x-restricted strategy
nodes.statement: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be a symmetric strategy the $(m+1,q,d)$-low individual degree test. Given $x \in \mathbb F_q$, we define the \emph{$x$-restricted strategy} $(\psi, A^x, B^x, L^x)$ for the $(m,q,d)$-low individual degree test as follows. \begin{enumerate} \item For each $u \in \mathbb F_q^m$, $(A^x)^u_a = A^{u, x}_a$. \item For each axis parallel line $\ell \in \mathbb F_q^m$, $(B^x)^\ell_f = B^{\mathrm{append}_x(\ell)}_{\mathrm{append}_x(f)}$. \item For each line $\ell \in \mathbb F_q^m$, $(L^x)^\ell_f = L^{\mathrm{append}_x(\ell)}_{\mathrm{append}_x(f)}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Restrict an (m+1)-variate symmetric strategy to the hyperplane with last coordinate x.

nodes.name: Restricted strategies inherit failure probabilities
nodes.statement: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m+1, d, q)$-low individual degree test. For each $x \in \mathbb F_q$, let $(\psi, A^x, B^x, L^x)$ be the corresponding $x$-restricted strategy. In addition, write $\epsilon_x$ for the probability that it fails the axis-parallel lines test, $\delta_x$ for the probability it fails the self-consistency test, and $\gamma_x$ for the probability it fails the diagonal lines test. Then \begin{equation*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \epsilon_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \leq \left(\frac{m+1}{m}\right) \cdot\epsilon, \quad \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \delta_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \leq \delta, \quad \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \gamma_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \leq \left(\frac{m+1}{m}\right) \cdot \gamma. \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m+1, d, q)$-low individual degree test.
For each $x \in \mathbb F_q$, let $(\psi, A^x, B^x, L^x)$ be the corresponding $x$-restricted strategy.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We begin with the self-consistency test. Here, both provers are given a uniformly random point $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}})$, they measure using $A^{\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}} = (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}})^{\boldsymbol{u}}$, and they succeed if their outcomes are the same. This is equivalent to performing the self-consistency test on the ${\boldsymbol{x}}$-restricted strategy, averaged over ${\boldsymbol{x}}$, and so $\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \delta_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \leq \delta$. (It is a ``$\leq$" rather than an ``$=$" because $\delta$ is just an upper-bound on the failure probability.) Next, we consider the axis-parallel lines test. Suppose the provers are sent the line $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ and the point $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}) \in \boldsymbol{\ell}$. With probability $\frac{1}{m+1}$, $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is parallel to the $(m+1)$-st direction. When it is not, then $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \mathrm{append}_x(\boldsymbol{\ell}')$, where $\boldsymbol{\ell}'$ is an axis-parallel line in $\mathbb F_q^m$. In this case, the points prover measures with the measurement $A^{\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}} = (A^{\boldsymbol{x}})^{\boldsymbol{u}}$ and receives an outcome $\boldsymbol{a}$, the lines prover measures with the measurement $B^{\boldsymbol{\ell}} = (B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}})^{\boldsymbol{\ell}'}$ and receives an outcome $\boldsymbol{f} = \mathrm{append}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}(\boldsymbol{f}')$, and they succeed if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}) = \boldsymbol{a}$, or, equivalently, if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$. Hence, the probability that they succeed is equal to the probability that the ${\boldsymbol{x}}$-restricted strategy passes the $(m, q, d)$-low individual degree test, which is $\epsilon_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}$. As a result, \begin{align*} \epsilon &\geq \mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}, \boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}}[\text{$A$ and $B$ succeed given $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}})$}]\\ &\geq \left(\frac{m}{m+1}\right) \cdot \mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}, \boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}}[\text{$A$ and $B$ succeed given $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}})$} \mid \text{$\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is not parallel to direction $m+1$}]\\ & = \left(\frac{m}{m+1}\right) \cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \epsilon_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}. \end{align*} Finally, the analysis of the diagonal lines test follows the same proof as the axis-parallel lines test, and we omit it here.
nodes.statement_short: Treat each subtest: self-consistency transfers directly; for lines not in the last direction the restricted strategy plays the same test.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
We note that the bound we are proving is trivial when at least one of $\epsilon$, $\delta$, $\gamma$, or $d/q$ is $\geq 1$, as $
u$ is at least~$1$ in that case. Hence, we may assume that $\epsilon, \delta, \gamma, d/q \leq 1$. This will aid us when carrying out the error calculations, as it allows us to bound terms like $(d/q)^{1/2}$ by terms like $(d/q)^{1/4}$. The proof is by induction on~$m$. The base case is when $m = 1$. In this case, there is only one axis-parallel line~$\ell$ in $\mathbb F_q^m$, and so $B^\ell \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$. Because this strategy fails the axis-parallel line test with probability at most~$\epsilon$,  egin{equation*} A^u_a \otimes I \simeq_{\epsilon} I \otimes B^\ell_{[f(u) = a]}, \end{equation*} on average over $ oldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q$. We note that this bound holds independent of the value of~$k$. This is even better than the theorem demands, and so the theorem is proved. Now we perform the induction step. Assuming that \Cref{thm:main-induction} holds for~$m \geq 1$, we will show that it holds for~$m+1$ as well. Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be an $(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma)$-good symmetric strategy for the $(m+1,q,d)$ low individual degree test. Let $k \geq (m+1)d$ be an integer. For each $x \in \mathbb F_q$, let $(\psi, A^x, B^x, L^x)$ be the corresponding $x$-restricted strategy. In addition, write $\epsilon_x$ for the probability that it fails the axis-parallel lines test, $\delta_x$ for the probability it fails the self-consistency test, and $\gamma_x$ for the probability it fails the diagonal lines test. For each $x \in \mathbb F_q$, we apply the inductive hypothesis to the $x$-restricted strategy with the same integer~$k$. This is possible because $k \geq (m+1)d \geq md$. Let  egin{equation*} 
u_x = 1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\Big(\epsilon_x^{1/1024} + \delta_x^{1/1024} + \gamma_x^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big), \end{equation*} and  egin{equation*} \sigma_x = m^2 \cdot\Big(
u_x + e^{- k/(80000m^2)}\Big) \end{equation*} Then the inductive hypothesis states that there exists a measurement $G^x \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ such that  egin{equation*} (A^x)^u_a\otimes I \simeq_{\sigma_x} I \otimes G^x_{[g(u)=a]}. \end{equation*} Next, we apply self-improvement to each~$G^x$. Let  egin{equation*} \zeta_x = 3000m \cdot \Big(\epsilon_x^{1/32} + \delta_x^{1/32} + (d/q)^{1/32}\Big). \end{equation*} Then \Cref{thm:self-improvement-in-induction-section} produces a projective sub-measurement $\widehat{G}^x \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$ such that for each $x \in \mathbb F_q$, the following statements hold.  egin{enumerate} \item(Completeness): If $\widehat{G}^x = \sum_g \widehat{G}^x_g$, then  egin{equation*}  ra{\psi} \widehat{G}^x \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\sigma_x) - \zeta_x. \end{equation*} \item(Consistency with~$A^x$): On average over $ oldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$,  egin{equation*} (A^x)^u_a \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta_x} I \otimes \widehat{G}^x_{[g(u) = a]}. \end{equation*} \item(Strong self-consistency):  egin{equation*} \widehat{G}^x_g \otimes I \approx_{\zeta_x} I \otimes \widehat{G}^x_g. \end{equation*} \item(Boundedness): There exists a positive-semidefinite matrix~$Z^x$ such that  egin{equation*}  ra{\psi} Z^x \otimes (I - \widehat{G}^x) \ket{\psi} \leq \zeta_x \end{equation*} and for each $g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$,  egin{equation*} Z^x \geq \Big( \mathop{ f E/}_{ oldsymbol{u}} (A^x)^{ oldsymbol{u}}_{g( oldsymbol{u})}\Big). \end{equation*} \end{enumerate} Having produced the $\widehat{G}^x$'s, we would like to paste them together. To do so, we need bounds for the above four properties which are stated on average over~${ oldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q$ rather than for each $x \in \mathbb F_q$ individually. This involves computing ``averaged" versions of our error parameters $
u_x$, $\sigma_x$, and $\zeta_x$. In these derivations, we will crucially use the fact that $\alpha \mapsto \alpha^c$ is concave when $c \leq 1$, and hence $\mathop{ f E/} ( oldsymbol{\alpha})^c \leq (\mathop{ f E/}  oldsymbol{\alpha})^c$.  egin{align*} \mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}}} 
u_{{ oldsymbol{x}}} & = \mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}}}\Big(1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\Big(\epsilon_{{ oldsymbol{x}}}^{1/1024} + \delta_{{ oldsymbol{x}}}^{1/1024} + \gamma_{{ oldsymbol{x}}}^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big)\Big)\ & \leq1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\Big((\mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}}}\epsilon_{{ oldsymbol{x}}})^{1/1024} + (\mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}}} \delta_{{ oldsymbol{x}}})^{1/1024} + (\mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}}}\gamma_{{ oldsymbol{x}}})^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big)	ag{by concavity}\ &\leq1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\Big(\Big( rac{(m+1)}{m} \cdot \epsilon\Big)^{1/1024} + \delta^{1/1024} + \Big( rac{(m+1)}{m} \cdot \gamma\Big)^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big) 	ag{by \Cref{lem:restricted-probabilities}}\ &\leq 1000k^2 (m+1)^2 \cdot\Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + \delta^{1/1024} + \gamma^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big). \end{align*} We call this value~$

nodes.name: Hypercube graph
nodes.statement: The \emph{hypercube graph} $C = (V,E)$ is the graph with vertex set $V = \mathbb F_q^m$ and an edge between $u, v \in V$ whenever $u$ and $v$ disagree in at most one coordinate (so that every vertex is connected to itself). A random edge in~$C$, denoted $(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C$, is distributed as follows: draw $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$, $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$, and ${\boldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q$, all uniformly at random, and set $\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{u} + {\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Graph on F_q^m joining points differing in at most one coordinate, with random edges given by an axis-parallel step.

nodes.name: Normalized adjacency matrix and Laplacian
nodes.statement: The \emph{normalized adjacency matrix of~$C$} is the matrix~$K$ defined as \begin{equation*} K = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}}. \end{equation*} The \emph{Laplacian of~$C$} is the matrix \begin{equation*} L = \frac{1}{M} \cdot I - K. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Laplacian as average of edge projectors
nodes.statement: $\displaystyle L = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} (\ket{\boldsymbol{u}} - \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}) \cdot (\bra{\boldsymbol{u}} - \bra{\boldsymbol{v}}).$
nodes.label: prop:laplacian-rewrite

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If we draw $(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C$, then both $\boldsymbol{u}$ and~$\boldsymbol{v}$ are distributed as uniformly random elements of~$\mathbb F_q^m$. As a result, \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{M} \cdot I = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{u}} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{u}} + \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}}. \end{equation*} In addition, $(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v})$ is distributed identically to $(\boldsymbol{v}, \boldsymbol{u})$. As a result, \begin{equation*} K = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}} + \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}\bra{\boldsymbol{u}}. \end{equation*} Combining these two, \begin{equation*} L = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \left[\ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{u}} + \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}} - \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}} - \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}\bra{\boldsymbol{u}}\right] = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} (\ket{\boldsymbol{u}} - \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}) \cdot (\bra{\boldsymbol{u}} - \bra{\boldsymbol{v}}).\qedhere \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Use that both endpoints of a random edge are uniform and that the edge distribution is symmetric.

nodes.name: Eigenvectors of the hypercube adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: For each $\alpha \in \mathbb F_q^m$, define the vector \begin{equation*} \ket{\varphi_\alpha} := \frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[u \cdot \alpha]}\cdot \ket{u}. \end{equation*} Then the following two statements are true. \begin{enumerate} \item The $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$'s form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^V$. \item For each $\alpha \in \mathbb F_q^m$, $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$ is an eigenvector for~$K$ with eigenvalue~$\frac{1}{M} \cdot \frac{m - |\alpha|}{m}$, where $|\alpha|$ is the number of nonzero coordinates in~$\alpha$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The characters phi_alpha form an orthonormal eigenbasis of K with eigenvalue (1/M)(m-|alpha|)/m.
assumptions: For each $\alpha \in \mathbb F_q^m$, define the vector
conclusions: The $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$'s form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^V$.
is an eigenvector for~$K$ with eigenvalue~$\frac{1}{M} \cdot \frac{m - |\alpha|}{m}$,
nodes.label: prop:eigenvectors

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First, we prove \Cref{item:orthonormal}. Given $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb F_q^m$, \begin{equation*} \braket{\varphi_\alpha \mid \varphi_\beta} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[u \cdot (\beta-\alpha)]} = \left\{\begin{array}{rl} 1 & \text{if } \alpha = \beta,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{array} \right.\tag{by~\Cref{prop:fourier-fact-vector}} \end{equation*} As a result, the $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$ vectors form an orthonormal basis of~$\mathbb C^V$. Next, we prove \Cref{item:eigenvector}. Given $\alpha \in \mathbb F_q^m$, \begin{equation} K \cdot \ket{\varphi_\alpha} = \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}}\right) \cdot \bigg(\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[u \cdot \alpha]}\cdot \ket{u}\bigg)\\ = \frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \alpha]} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}. \end{equation} By definition of a random edge, we can replace~$\boldsymbol{v}$ with $\boldsymbol{u} + {\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}}$, where $\boldsymbol{i}$ is a uniformly random index in $\{1, \ldots, m\}$ and ${\boldsymbol{x}}$ is a uniformly random element of $\mathbb F_q$. As a result, \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:eigenvector-calculation} = \frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{i}, {\boldsymbol{x}}} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[(\boldsymbol{u} + {\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}}) \cdot \alpha]} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}} = \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i}, {\boldsymbol{x}}}\omega^{\mathrm{tr}[({\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}}) \cdot \alpha]}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[\boldsymbol{u} \cdot \alpha]} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}} = \frac{1}{M}\left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i}, {\boldsymbol{x}}}\omega^{\mathrm{tr}[{\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot \alpha_{\boldsymbol{i}}]}\right) \cdot \ket{\varphi_\alpha}. \end{equation*} Hence, $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$ is an eigenvector of~$K$ with eigenvalue \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{M} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i}} \left[\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\omega^{\mathrm{tr}[{\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot \alpha_{\boldsymbol{i}}]}\right] = \frac{1}{M} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i}} \left[\boldsymbol{1}[\alpha_{\boldsymbol{i}} = 0]\right] = \frac{1}{M} \cdot \frac{m - |\alpha|}{m}. \tag{by~\Cref{prop:fourier-fact-scalar}} \end{equation*} This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormality from the vector character sum; eigenvalue by averaging the character over a random axis-parallel step.

nodes.name: Equation (47)
nodes.statement: K \cdot \ket{\varphi_\alpha} = \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}\bra{\boldsymbol{v}}\right) \cdot \bigg(\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[u \cdot \alpha]}\cdot \ket{u}\bigg)\\ = \frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \alpha]} \ket{\boldsymbol{u}}.
nodes.label: eq:eigenvector-calculation

nodes.name: Spectral gap of the hypercube Laplacian
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_M$ be the eigenvalues of~$L$. Then $\lambda_1 = 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \frac{1}{m M}$.
assumptions: Let $\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_M$ be the eigenvalues of~$L$.
nodes.label: cor:laplacian-spectral-gap

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\mu_1 \geq \mu_2 \geq \cdots \geq \mu_M$ be the eigenvalues of~$K$. Then $\mu_i = \frac{1}{M} - \lambda_i$. Thus, it suffices to show that $\mu_1 = \frac{1}{M}$ and $\mu_2 = \frac{1}{M} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m}$. By \Cref{prop:eigenvectors}, $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$ has eigenvalue $\frac{1}{M}$ when $|\alpha| = 0$ and eigenvalue $\frac{1}{M} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m}$ when $|\alpha| =1$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate to eigenvalues of K and read off the two largest from the eigenvector proposition.

nodes.name: Local and global variance
nodes.statement: The \emph{local variance of~$A$ on $\ket{\psi}$} is defined as \begin{equation*} \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{local}}(A, \psi):=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \bra{\psi} (A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}})^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*} The \emph{global variance of~$A$ on $\ket{\psi}$} is defined as \begin{equation*} \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{global}}(A, \psi):=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v} \sim \mathbb F_q^m} \bra{\psi} (A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}})^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Local variance averages (A^u - A^v)^2 over hypercube edges; global variance over independent uniform pairs.
nodes.label: def:local-and-variance

nodes.name: Local-to-global variance
nodes.statement: $\displaystyle \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{global}}(A, \psi) \leq m \cdot \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{local}}(A,\psi). $
nodes.label: lem:local-to-global

nodes.name: Local variance via the Laplacian
nodes.statement: Define the matrix \begin{equation*} A_{\mathrm{combine}} = \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{u} \otimes A^u \otimes I. \end{equation*} Then \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Tr}(A_{\mathrm{combine}}^\dagger \cdot (L \otimes \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}) \cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}})= \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{local}}(A, \psi). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Define the matrix
nodes.label: lem:local-rewrite

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For any $u, v \in \mathbb F_q^m$, \begin{align} ((\bra{u} - \bra{v}) \otimes \bra{\psi})\cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}} &= ((\bra{u} - \bra{v}) \otimes \bra{\psi})\cdot \sum_{w \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{w} \otimes A^w \otimes I\nonumber\\ &= \bra{\psi}\cdot ((A^u- A^v) \otimes I). \end{align} As a result, \begin{align*} &A_{\mathrm{combine}}^\dagger \cdot L \otimes \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi} \cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}}\\ =~& \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} A_{\mathrm{combine}}^\dagger ((\ket{\boldsymbol{u}} - \ket{\boldsymbol{v}}) \cdot (\bra{\boldsymbol{u}} - \bra{\boldsymbol{v}})\otimes \ket{\psi} \bra{\psi})\cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}}\tag{by \Cref{prop:laplacian-rewrite}}\\ =~& \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} ((A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}}) \otimes I) \cdot \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi} \cdot ((A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}}) \otimes I). \tag{by \eqref{eq:reader-probably-has-no-idea-whats-going-on-yet}} \end{align*} Thus, if we take the trace, \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Tr}(A_{\mathrm{combine}}^\dagger \cdot (L \otimes \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}) \cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}}) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v}) \sim C} \bra{\psi} (A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}})^2 \otimes I \cdot \ket{\psi} = \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{local}}(A, \psi). \end{equation*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the Laplacian as an average over edges and take the trace.

nodes.name: Equation (48)
nodes.statement: ((\bra{u} - \bra{v}) \otimes \bra{\psi})\cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}} &= ((\bra{u} - \bra{v}) \otimes \bra{\psi})\cdot \sum_{w \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{w} \otimes A^w \otimes I\nonumber\\ &= \bra{\psi}\cdot ((A^u- A^v) \otimes I).
nodes.label: eq:reader-probably-has-no-idea-whats-going-on-yet

nodes.name: Global variance via the non-constant component
nodes.statement: Expand $A_{\mathrm{combine}}$ as \begin{equation*} A_{\mathrm{combine}} = \ket{\varphi_0} \otimes A_0 + \ket{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp}, \end{equation*} where $\ket{\varphi_{\perp}}$ is orthogonal to $\ket{\varphi_0}$. (Here we are writing $\ket{\varphi_0}$ for the vector $\ket{\varphi_\alpha}$ from \Cref{prop:eigenvectors} in the case of $\alpha = (0, \ldots, 0)$.) Then \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{M} \cdot \mathrm{Tr}(\bra{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}) \cdot \ket{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp})= \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{global}}(A, \psi). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Expand $A_{\mathrm{combine}}$ as
nodes.label: lem:global-rewrite

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We begin by computing~$A_0$: \begin{equation*} A_0 = \bra{\varphi_0} \otimes I \cdot A_{\mathrm{combine}} = \bigg(\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \bra{u}\bigg) \otimes I \cdot \bigg(\sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{u} \otimes A^u \otimes I\bigg) = \frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} A^u \otimes I. \end{equation*} Then \begin{align*} \ket{\varphi_0} \otimes A_0 = \bigg(\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{u}\bigg)\otimes \bigg(\frac{1}{M^{1/2}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} A^u \otimes I\bigg) &= \frac{1}{M} \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{u} \otimes \sum_{v \in \mathbb F_q^m} A^v \otimes I\\ &= \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} \ket{u} \otimes A_{\mathrm{avg}} \otimes I, \end{align*} where we have written $A_{\mathrm{avg}} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}$. As a result, \begin{equation*} \ket{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp} = A_{\mathrm{combine}} - \ket{\varphi_0} \otimes A_0 = \sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^n} \ket{u} \otimes (A^u - A_{\mathrm{avg}}) \otimes I. \end{equation*} Thus, \begin{align*} &\bra{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}) \cdot \ket{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp}\\ =&\sum_{u, v \in \mathbb F_q^m} \braket{u \mid v} \otimes ((A^u - A_{\mathrm{avg}}) \otimes I) \cdot \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi} \cdot ((A^v - A_{\mathrm{avg}}) \otimes I)\\ =&\sum_{u \in \mathbb F_q^m} ((A^u - A_{\mathrm{avg}}) \otimes I) \cdot \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi} \cdot ((A^u - A_{\mathrm{avg}}) \otimes I). \end{align*} As a result, if we take the trace, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{M} \cdot \mathrm{Tr}(\bra{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}) \cdot \ket{\varphi_{\perp}} \otimes A_{\perp}) = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m} \bra{\psi} (A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} We can rewrite the squared expression as \begin{align*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m}(A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2 &= \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m}((A^{\boldsymbol{u}})^2 + (A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2 - A^{\boldsymbol{u}} \cdot A_{\mathrm{avg}} - A_{\mathrm{avg}} \cdot A^{\boldsymbol{u}})\\ &= \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m}((A^{\boldsymbol{u}})^2 - (A_{\mathrm{avg}})^2)\\ &= \frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v} \sim \mathbb F_q^m}((A^{\boldsymbol{u}})^2 + (A^{\boldsymbol{v}})^2 - A^{\boldsymbol{u}} \cdot A^{\boldsymbol{v}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}} \cdot A^{\boldsymbol{u}})\\ &= \frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v} \sim \mathbb F_q^m}(A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}})^2. \end{align*} Thus, \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:just-took-trace} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{v} \sim \mathbb F_q^m} \bra{\psi} (A^{\boldsymbol{u}} - A^{\boldsymbol{v}})^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \mathbf{Var}_{\mathrm{global}}(A, \psi). \end{equation*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: To show that~\eqref{eq:primal-objective} and~\eqref{eq:dual-objective} are dual to each other, we begin by rewriting the primal~\eqref{eq:primal-objective} in canonical form. Let $r$ be the dimension of the space on which~$A$ acts. Let $M = |\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}|$ be the number of polynomials with individual degree $d$. We will assume some ordering of these polynomials $g_1, \ldots, g_M \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ which is allowed to be arbitrary. Consider the following semidefinite program: \begin{align} \sup &\quad \mathrm{tr}(C^\dagger X) \\ \text{s.t.} &\quad \mathrm{tr}(D_{ij}^\dagger X) = b_{ij} \qquad\forall i,j\in\{1,\ldots,r\},\nonumber\\ &\quad X \geq 0,\nonumber \end{align} where the variables~$C$, $D_{ij}$, and $b_{ij}$ are defined as follows: \begin{equation*} C = \sum_{i = 1}^M \ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes A_{g_i} \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} \forall i,j \in [r], \quad D_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{M+1} \ket{k}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{i}\bra{j}, \qquad b_{ij} = \left\{\begin{array}{rl} 1 & \text{if } i = j,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} We claim that \eqref{eq:primal-canonical} is equivalent to \eqref{eq:primal-objective}. To see this, let \begin{equation*} X = \sum_{i, j =1}^{M+1} \ket{i}\bra{j} \otimes X_{ij} \end{equation*} be a feasible solution to \eqref{eq:primal-canonical}. Then because $X \geq 0$, $X_{i i} \geq 0$ for each $i \in [M+1]$. In addition \begin{align*} \mathrm{tr}(D_{i_1 i_2}^\dagger X) &= \sum_k \sum_{j_1 j_2} \mathrm{tr}((\ket{k}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{i_1}\bra{i_2})\cdot(\ket{j_1} \bra{j_2} \otimes X_{j_1 j_2}))\\ &= \sum_k \bra{i_2} X_{k k} \ket{i_1}\\ &= \left\{\begin{array}{rl} 1 & \text{if } i_1 = i_2,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{array}\right. \end{align*} This is equivalent to the statement $\sum_{i=1}^{M+1} X_{i i} = I$, which implies that $\sum_{i=1}^M X_{i i} \leq I$. Finally, the objective value \eqref{eq:primal-canonical} is \begin{align*} \mathrm{tr}(C^\dagger X) & = \sum_{i = 1}^M \sum_{j,k = 1}^{M+1} \mathrm{tr}((\ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes A_{g_i}^\dagger) \cdot (\ket{j}\bra{k} \otimes X_{j, k}))\\ &= \sum_{i = 1}^M \mathrm{tr}(A_{g_i}^\dagger \cdot X_{i, i})\\ &= \sum_{i = 1}^M \mathrm{tr}(A_{g_i} \cdot X_{i, i}). \tag{because~$A$ is Hermitian} \end{align*} As a result, setting $T_{g_i} = X_{i i}$ for each $i \in [M]$ gives a feasible solution to the original semidefinite program~\eqref{eq:primal-objective} with a matching objective value. A similar transformation allows us to convert solutions of~\eqref{eq:primal-objective} to~\eqref{eq:primal-canonical}. The dual of \eqref{eq:primal-canonical} is \begin{align} \inf &\quad \sum_i\, z_{ij} b_{ij} \\ \text{s.t.} &\quad \sum_{i,j} \,z_{ij} D_{ij} \geq C. \end{align} We claim that \eqref{eq:dual-canonical} is equivalent to \eqref{eq:dual-objective}. To see this, we first calculate \begin{align*} \sum_{i,j=1}^r \,z_{ij} D_{ij} = \sum_{i,j=1}^r z_{ij} \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{M+1} \ket{k}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{i}\bra{j} &= \sum_{k=1}^{M+1} \ket{k}\bra{k} \otimes \left(\sum_{i, j=1}^r z_{ij}\ket{i}\bra{j}\right)\\ &=: \sum_{k=1}^{M+1}\ket{k}\bra{k} \otimes Z. \end{align*} Then the constraint \eqref{eq:dual-canonical-constraint} states that \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^{M+1}\ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes Z \geq C = \sum_{i = 1}^M \ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes A_{g_i}, \end{equation*} which is equivalent to the statement that $Z \geq A_{g_i}$ for all $i \in [M]$ and $Z \geq 0$. In other words, $Z$ is a feasible solution to the original dual SDP \eqref{eq:dual-objective}, with value \begin{equation*} \mathrm{tr}(Z) = \sum_{i=1}^r Z_{i i} = \sum_{i,j=1}^r b_{i j} Z_{i j} = \sum_{i,j=1}^r b_{i j} z_{i j}, \end{equation*} the same value as in \eqref{eq:dual-canonical}. Hence, the two dual programs are the same as well, which implies that \eqref{eq:primal-objective} and \eqref{eq:dual-objective} form a primal/dual pair. To show that a primal/dual pair satisfies \emph{strong duality}, i.e.\ that their optimum values are the same, we use Slater's condition~\cite[Section~5.2.3]{cvxbook} and show that they satisfy \emph{strict feasibility}, which means both have a feasible solution which is positive \emph{definite} that satisfies all constraints with a strict inequality. It can be checked that the following two solutions to \eqref{eq:primal-objective} and \eqref{eq:dual-objective} satisfy this property: \begin{equation*} \forall g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}, \quad T_g = \frac{1}{2M} \cdot I, \qquad\qquad\qquad Z = 2I. \end{equation*} Because they satisfy strong duality, their optimal solutions satisfy the \emph{complementary slackness} condition (see~\cite{AHO97}). If $X$ and $(z_{ij})$ are an optimal pair of solutions to~\eqref{eq:primal-canonical} and~\eqref{eq:dual-canonical} respectively, this implies that \begin{equation} X\Big( \sum_{i,j} \,z_{ij} D_{ij} - C \Big) \,=\, 0 \;. \end{equation} Clearly for any optimal pair $(X,z_{ij})$ we can assume without loss of generality that $X$ is block-diagonal. Then if we translate \eqref{eq:complementary-slackness} back to the variables $\{T_g\}$ and $Z$, we get \begin{align*} 0 = X\Big( \sum_{i,j} \,z_{ij} D_{ij} - C \Big) &= \sum_{i=1}^{M+1} \ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes X_{ii} \cdot \bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{M+1} \ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes Z - \sum_{i=1}^M \ket{i}\bra{i}\otimes A_{g_i}\bigg)\\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{M} \ket{i}\bra{i} \otimes (X_{ii} \cdot (Z - A_{g_i})) + \ket{M+1}\bra{M+1} \otimes (X_{M+1,M+1} \cdot Z). \end{align*} This implies that $X_{ii} \cdot (Z - A_{g_i}) = 0$ for $i \in [M]$ and $X_{M+1, M+1} = 0$. Translating back to the variables $\{T_g\}$ and $Z$, this gives $T_g(Z-A_g)=0$ for all $g\in\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ and $\sum_g T_g = I$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the primal in canonical SDP form, compute its dual, check both reduce to the stated programs, then use Slater's condition and complementary slackness.
