nodes.statement: On the other hand, we know of a quantum strategy using noncommuting measurements which succeeds with probability~$1$ in the $m = 2$, $d = 2$, $q = 4$ low individual degree test.

nodes.name: The (m,q,d)-low individual degree test
nodes.statement: With probability~$\tfrac{1}{3}$ each, perform one of the following three tests. \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Axis-parallel lines test:} Pick a uniformly random role $\boldsymbol{r} \sim \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. Select $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$ uniformly at random, and let $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \{\boldsymbol{u} + t \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}} \mid t \in \mathbb F_q\}$ be the axis-parallel line which passes through~$\boldsymbol{u}$ in the $\boldsymbol{i}$-th direction. \begin{itemize} \item[$\circ$] Player~$\boldsymbol{r}$: Give $\boldsymbol{\ell}$; receive the univariate degree-$d$ polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{\ell} \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$. \item[$\circ$] Player~$\overline{\boldsymbol{r}}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$. \end{itemize} Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$. \item \textbf{Self-consistency test:} Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. \begin{itemize} \item[$\circ$] Player~$\mathrm{A}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$. \item[$\circ$] Player~$\mathrm{B}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb F_q$. \end{itemize} Accept if $\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{b}$. \item \textbf{Diagonal lines test:} Pick a uniformly random role $\boldsymbol{r} \sim \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. Select $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$ uniformly at random, and let $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point whose last $m - \boldsymbol{i}$ coordinates are~$0$. Finally, let $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \{\boldsymbol{u} + t \cdot \boldsymbol{v} \mid t \in \mathbb F_q\}$ be the line which passes through~$\boldsymbol{u}$ in direction~$\boldsymbol{v}$. \begin{itemize} \item[$\circ$] Player~$\boldsymbol{r}$: Give $\boldsymbol{\ell}$; receive the univariate degree-$md$ polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{\ell} \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$. \item[$\circ$] Player~$\overline{\boldsymbol{r}}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$. \end{itemize} Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: Verifier runs, with probability 1/3 each, the axis-parallel lines test, the self-consistency test, or the diagonal lines test.

nodes.name: Approximate equality of complex numbers
nodes.statement: For two complex numbers $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb C$, we write $\alpha \approx_{\epsilon} \beta$ if \begin{equation*} |\alpha - \beta| \leq \epsilon.

nodes.name: Finite field
nodes.statement: A \emph{finite field} is a field with a finite number of elements.
differentia: with a finite number of elements

nodes.name: Classification of finite fields
nodes.statement: There is a unique finite field~$\mathbb F_q$ of~$q$ elements for each prime power $q = p^t$, and there are no other finite fields.
conclusions: There is a unique finite field~$\mathbb F_q$ of~$q$ elements for each prime power $q = p^t$
and there are no other finite fields

nodes.name: Root of unity omega
nodes.statement: We write $\omega$ for the $p$-th root of unity $\omega = e^{2 \pi i/p}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Schwartz-Zippel for individual degree
nodes.statement: Since any polynomial with individual degree~$d$ has total degree~$md$, \Cref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} implies the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Individual degree d implies total degree md; apply Schwartz-Zippel.

nodes.name: Incomplete part of a sub-measurement
nodes.statement: The complete part of a sub-measurement contrasts with its \emph{incomplete part}, which is the matrix $I - A^x$.

nodes.name: Differences from the NW19 definition of consistency
nodes.statement: We note that there are two differences between the definition of consistency in \Cref{def:simeq} and the original definition of consistency given in \cite[Definition 4.11]{NW19}. The first of these is that the~\cite{NW19} definition allows the right-hand side of \Cref{eq:no-big-Oh} to be $O(\delta)$ rather than strictly~$\delta$. The benefit of this is that they do not need to keep track of constant prefactors in their proofs; we have elected to use this more concrete definition to make our proofs more easily verifiable, at the expense of tracking these constant prefactors. The second difference is that is that they define their consistency as the quantity \begin{equation*} 1 - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*} As we show below in \Cref{prop:simeq-for-measurements}, this agrees with \Cref{def:simeq} when~$A$ and~$B$ are both measurements. However, these two definitions disagree when~$A$ and~$B$ are \emph{sub}-measurements, which is a case we will frequently encounter throughout this paper.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike NW19, consistency here is an exact bound (no big-O) and counts disagreements rather than 1 minus agreement, which matters for sub-measurements.

nodes.name: Proof strategy of chained approximations
nodes.statement: In this strategy, we would like to demonstrate a sequence of expressions in which each expression is close to the previous one: \begin{equation*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_0)^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a (B_0)^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \approx_{\epsilon_1} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_1)^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a (B_1)^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \approx_{\epsilon_2} \cdots \approx_{\epsilon_t} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_t)^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a (B_t)^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*} By the triangle inequality, we can therefore conclude that the $0$-th expression is close to the $t$-th expression. To show that the $i$-th quantity is close to the $(i+1)$-st, we will typically arrange for $A_{i} = A_{i+1}$, and we will swap out $B_i$ for $B_{i+1}$ using an approximation relation such as $(B_i)^x_a \approx (B_{i+1})^x_a$, with the help of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (or the same might occur with the roles of~$A$ and~$B$ reversed). Even if $A_0$ and $B_0$ can be written as local measurements applied to either side of a bipartition, e.g.\ $(A_0)^x_a = A^x_a \otimes I$ and $(B_0)^x_a = I \otimes B^x_a$, and likewise for $A_t$ and $B_t$, the intermediate steps may feature matrices which do not decompose nicely across a bipartition. This is why \Cref{def:approx_delta} is phrased so broadly, with no mention of a bipartition.
nodes.section: 4.4.3 Deriving consistency relations from the state-dependent distance
nodes.statement_short: Proofs proceed through a chain of approximately equal expressions, swapping one operator at a time via Cauchy-Schwarz; intermediate operators need not be bipartite.

nodes.name: Self-consistency
nodes.statement: It seems natural to study this using \emph{self-consistency} of~$A$, i.e. the number~$\delta$ such that \begin{equation*} A^x_a \otimes I \simeq_{\delta} I \otimes A^x_a.

nodes.name: Strong self-consistency for projective sub-measurements
nodes.statement: Hence, we may also refer to the condition $A^x_a \otimes I \approx_{2\delta} I \otimes A^x_a$ as ``strong self-consistency'' if~$A$ is projective.

nodes.name: Closeness does not imply consistency for non-projective measurements
nodes.statement: On the other hand when~$A$ and~$B$ are not projective, one can find examples of measurements where $A^x_a \otimes I \approx_{\delta} I \otimes B^x_a$ for $\delta \rightarrow 0$ but one can show $A^x_a \otimes I \simeq_{\epsilon} I \otimes B^x_a$ only for $\epsilon \rightarrow 1$; this is Remark~$4.15$ from~\cite{NW19}.

nodes.name: Naimark dilation does not preserve state-dependent closeness
nodes.statement: However, there is subtlety in doing so, which is that Naimark dilation does not necessarily preserve ``$\approx_{\delta}$" statements; in other words, $A^x_a \otimes I \approx_{\delta} I \otimes B^x_a$ does not necessarily imply $\widehat{A}^x_a \otimes I \approx_{\delta} I \otimes \widehat{B}^x_a$.
conclusions: Naimark dilation does not necessarily preserve ``$\approx_{\delta}$" statements

nodes.name: Number of vertices M
nodes.statement: We will use $M$ to denote the number of vertices in~$C$, i.e.\ $M = q^m$.

nodes.name: Setting for local and global variance
nodes.statement: In this section, $\ket{\psi}$ will denote a vector (not necessarily normalized) in $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$, and for each $u \in \mathbb F_q^m$, $0 \leq A^u \leq I$ will be a matrix acting on $\mathcal{H}_A$.

nodes.name: Self-improvement: completeness
nodes.statement: (Completeness): If $H = \sum_h H_h$, then \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} H \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\nu)-\zeta. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Self-improvement: consistency with A
nodes.statement: (Consistency with~$A$): On average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$, \begin{equation*} A^u_a \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta} I \otimes H_{[h(u) = a]}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Self-improvement: strong self-consistency
nodes.statement: (Strong self-consistency): \begin{equation*} \sum_{h} \bra{\psi} H_h \otimes H_h \ket{\psi} \geq \bra{\psi} H \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \zeta. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Self-improvement: boundedness
nodes.statement: (Boundedness): There exists a positive-semidefinite matrix~$Z$ such that \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Z \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}_{a} \otimes H_{[h(\boldsymbol{u})=a]} \ket{\psi} \leq \zeta \end{equation*} and for each $h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, \begin{equation*} Z \geq \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}_{h(\boldsymbol{u})}\right). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Shorthand A_g
nodes.statement: To define them, it will be convenient to introduce the notational shorthand \begin{equation*} A_g = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}_{g(\boldsymbol{u})}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Primal and dual semidefinite programs for self-improvement
nodes.statement: Then the primal is \begin{align} \sup &\quad \sum_g \,\mathrm{tr}(T_g \cdot A_g) \\ \text{s.t.} &\quad T_g \geq 0\qquad\forall g\in\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}\;,\notag\\ &\quad \sum_g T_g \leq I,\notag \end{align} and the dual is \begin{align} \inf &\quad \mathrm{tr}(Z) \\ \text{ s.t.} &\quad Z \geq A_g. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Primal: maximize sum_g tr(T_g A_g) over sub-measurements T; dual: minimize tr(Z) subject to Z >= A_g.

nodes.name: Construction of H for self-improvement
nodes.statement: We let $T = \{T_g\}$ and $Z$ be the optimal solutions to the SDPs~\eqref{eq:primal-objective} and \eqref{eq:dual-objective} respectively given by \Cref{lem:sdp}. Then~$T$ is a measurement, and \begin{align} \forall g \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}: \qquad Z &\geq (\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}_{g(\boldsymbol{u})}), \\ T_g \cdot Z &= T_g \cdot (\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u}} A^{\boldsymbol{u}}_{g(\boldsymbol{u})}). \end{align} For each $u \in \mathbb F_q^m$, define $H^u = \{H^u_h\}_{h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}}$ as \begin{equation*} H^u_h := A^u_{h(u)}\cdot T_h \cdot A^u_{h(u)}. \end{equation*} Let $u \in \mathbb F_q^m$. Then \begin{align*} \sum_{h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} H^u_h & = \sum_{h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} A^u_{h(u)} \cdot T_h \cdot A^u_{h(u)}\\ & = \sum_{a \in \mathbb F_q}A^u_{a} \cdot \bigg(\sum_{h:h(u) = a} T_h\bigg) \cdot A^u_{a}\\ & \leq \sum_{a \in \mathbb F_q} (A^u_{a})^2\tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ & = \sum_{a \in \mathbb F_q} A^u_{a}\tag{$A$ is projective}\\ & = I. \end{align*} Hence, $H^u$ is a sub-measurement, and therefore $H^u \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$. Next, define $H = \{H_h\}_{h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}}$ as \begin{equation*} H_h := \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m}H^{\boldsymbol{u}}_h. \end{equation*} Then \begin{equation*} \sum_{h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} H_h = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m} \sum_{h \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}} H^{\boldsymbol{u}}_h \leq I. \tag{$H^u$ is a sub-measurement} \end{equation*} Hence, $H$ is a sub-measurement, and therefore $H \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$. Set \begin{equation*} \zeta_{\mathrm{variance}} = 24m\cdot\Big(\epsilon + \delta + \frac{md}{q}\Big) \end{equation*} to be the error in \Cref{eq:local-variance-of-points-equation}. Prior to showing that~$H$ satisfies \Cref{item:self-improvement-A-consistency,item:self-improvement-completeness,item:self-improvement-self,item:self-improvement-boundedness}, we will prove the following technical lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Take optimal SDP solutions T,Z; define H^u_h = A^u_{h(u)} T_h A^u_{h(u)} and H_h its average over u, both sub-measurements.

nodes.name: Consistency relations used in pasting
nodes.statement_short: Derives from the hypotheses of the pasting theorem that A, B and G are mutually consistent in the last direction and that the G^x commute.

nodes.name: First pasting construction
nodes.statement: The first construction of $H = \{H_h\}$ is conceptually simple: we perform the $G$ sub-measurement $d+1$ times to produce $d+1$ polynomials $g_1, \ldots, g_{d+1} \in \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$. We then perform polynomial interpolation to produce a single global polynomial $h \in \polyfunc{m+1}{q}{d}$. In more detail, this construction involves three steps. \begin{enumerate} \item (Pasting): Let $x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1} \in \mathbb F_q$. We will define an initial ``sandwiched" measurement as follows: \begin{equation*} \widehat{H}^{x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}}_{g_1, \ldots, g_{d+1}} = G^{x_1}_{g_1} \cdot G^{x_2}_{g_2} \cdots G^{x_{d+1}}_{g_{d+1}} \cdots G^{x_2}_{g_2} \cdot G^{x_1}_{g_1}. \end{equation*} $\widehat{H}^{x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}}$ has a natural interpretation as the sub-measurement in which one performs the sub-measurements $G^{x_1}, G^{x_2}, \ldots, G^{x_{d+1}}$ one after another and outputs their results. \item (Interpolation) Next, let $(x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}) \in \distinct{d+1}$. We define the interpolated measurement \begin{equation*} H^{x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}}_{h} = \widehat{H}^{x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}}_{h|_{x_1}, \ldots, h|_{x_{d+1}}}. \end{equation*} This performs the $\widehat{H}^{x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}}$ measurement and outputs the~$h$ which is consistent with the outcomes~$g_1, \ldots, g_{d+1}$ if one exists. (We note that this is not necessarily a sub-measurement if $(x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1}) \notin \distinct{d+1}$. This is because there may exist $h \neq h'$ for which $h|_{x_i} = (h')|_{x_i}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq d+1$.) \item (Averaging): Finally, we randomize over the choice of $(x_1, \ldots, x_{d+1})$. In other words, we define \begin{equation*} H_{h} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{({\boldsymbol{x}}_1, \ldots, {\boldsymbol{x}}_{d+1}) \sim \distinct{d+1}} H^{{\boldsymbol{x}}_1, \ldots, {\boldsymbol{x}}_{d+1}}_h. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Measure G at d+1 points sequentially, interpolate the outcomes into a global polynomial, and average over distinct points.

nodes.name: First construction preserves completeness for constant d
nodes.statement: However, we can show \Cref{eq:subtract-a-G} is actually correct and therefore this ``naive analysis" is incorrect, at least in the case of constant~$d$.

nodes.name: Sketch for the first construction
nodes.statement: We now sketch the argument that shows this holds, at least for constant~$d$. To do this, it is first possible to show that \begin{equation} \bra{\psi} G^{d+2} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{\Delta} \bra{\psi} G^{d+1} \otimes I \ket{\psi}, \end{equation} where $\Delta = \mathrm{poly}(m) \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma, \zeta, d/q)$ is small. Intuitively, this is because after performing $(d+1)$ $G$ measurements, the outcome of another $G$ measurement is essentially determined due to interpolation. (The proof is of this fact is slightly subtle and involves the $Z$-boundedness condition.) From here, it is possible to derive \Cref{eq:subtract-a-G} as follows. Write the eigendecomposition $G = \sum_i \lambda_i \ket{v_i}\bra{v_i}$ of~$G$. This defines a probability distribution $\mu$ over eigenvectors, where eigenvector~$i$ occurs with probability $\mu(i) = \bra{\psi} (\ket{v_i}\bra{v_i} \otimes I) \ket{\psi}$. In this language, for any power~$k$ we can write \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} G^k \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \bra{\psi} \Big(\sum_i \lambda_i^k \ket{v_i}\bra{v_i}\Big) \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \sum_i \lambda_i^k \cdot \mu(i) = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim \mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^k]. \end{equation*} Thus, \Cref{eq:step-one-of-grand-plan} is equivalent to the statement that \begin{equation} \Delta \geq \bra{\psi} G^{d+1} \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \bra{\psi} G^{d+2} \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim \mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{d+1}] - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim \mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{d+2}] = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim\mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{d+1}(1-\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}})]. \end{equation} By \Cref{eq:subtract-a-G}, our goal is to bound \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} G \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \bra{\psi} G^{d+1} \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim \mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}] - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim \mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{d+1}] = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim\mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}(1-\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^d)]. \end{equation*} To do so, we will use the following lemma. \begin{lemma} For any real number $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$, \begin{equation*} \lambda (1-\lambda^d) \leq 2 \cdot \Big(\lambda^{d+1}(1-\lambda)\Big)^{1/(d+1)}. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} The lemma is trivial for $\lambda = 1$, and so we will assume that $\lambda \neq 1$. We note that \begin{align*} \lambda^{d+1} (1-\lambda^d)^{d+1} \leq \lambda^{d+1} (1-\lambda^d) &= \lambda^{d+1}(1-\lambda) \cdot \left(\frac{1-\lambda^d}{1-\lambda}\right)\\ &= \lambda^{d+1}(1-\lambda) \cdot (1 + \lambda + \cdots + \lambda^{d-1}) \leq d \cdot \lambda^{d+1}(1-\lambda). \end{align*} The lemma now follows by taking the $(d+1)$-st root of both sides and noting that $d^{1/(d+1)} \leq 2$ for all integers $d \geq 1$. \end{proof} Then \Cref{lem:looks-easy-but-took-me-a-while} implies that \begin{align*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim\mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}(1-\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^d)] &\leq 2\cdot \mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim\mu}\Big[\Big(\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{d+1}(1-\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}})\Big)^{1/(d+1)}\Big]\\ &\leq2\cdot \Big(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{\boldsymbol{i} \sim\mu}[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{d+1}(1-\lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}})]\Big)^{1/(d+1)} \tag{because $a \mapsto a^{1/(d+1)}$ is concave}\\ &\leq 2 \cdot \Delta^{1/(d+1)}. \tag{by \Cref{eq:equivalent-way-of-writing-grand-plan}} \end{align*} Thus, we have established the bound \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi}G \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \bra{\psi}G^{d+1} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 2\cdot \Delta^{1/{d+1}} = 2\cdot ( \mathrm{poly}(m) \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon, \delta, \gamma, \zeta,d/q))^{1/{d+1}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: G^{d+2} ~ G^{d+1} by interpolation, then an eigenvalue argument with a scalar inequality shows G^{d+1} ~ G up to Delta^{1/(d+1)}.

nodes.name: Introduce the test and its parameter k
nodes.statement: In this setting, the surface-versus-point low degree test, parameterized by an integer $k \geq 1$, is performed by the verifier as follows.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the test and its parameter k

nodes.name: Sample a point and query Prover A
nodes.statement: Select~$\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ uniformly at random. Give it to Prover~$\mathrm{A}$. They respond with a value~$\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Sample a point and query Prover A

nodes.name: Sample a surface through the point and query Prover B
nodes.statement: Select a uniformly random $k$-dimensional affine surface~$\boldsymbol{s}$ in~$\mathbb F_q^m$ containing~$\boldsymbol{u}$. Give it to Prover~$\mathrm{B}$. They respond with a degree-$d$ $k$-variate polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{s}\rightarrow \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Sample a surface through the point and query Prover B

nodes.name: Accept iff answers agree
nodes.statement: Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$.

nodes.name: Choose one of three subtests uniformly
nodes.statement: With probability~$\tfrac{1}{3}$ each, perform one of the following three tests.
nodes.statement_short: Choose one of three subtests uniformly

nodes.name: Axis-parallel lines test
nodes.statement: \textbf{Axis-parallel lines test:} Pick a uniformly random role $\boldsymbol{r} \sim \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. Select $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$ uniformly at random, and let $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \{\boldsymbol{u} + t \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}} \mid t \in \mathbb F_q\}$ be the axis-parallel line which passes through~$\boldsymbol{u}$ in the $\boldsymbol{i}$-th direction. \begin{itemize} \item[$\circ$] Player~$\boldsymbol{r}$: Give $\boldsymbol{\ell}$; receive the univariate degree-$d$ polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{\ell} \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$. \item[$\circ$] Player~$\overline{\boldsymbol{r}}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$. \end{itemize} Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$.

nodes.name: Sample role, point and axis direction
nodes.statement: \textbf{Axis-parallel lines test:} Pick a uniformly random role $\boldsymbol{r} \sim \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. Select $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$ uniformly at random, and let $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \{\boldsymbol{u} + t \cdot e_{\boldsymbol{i}} \mid t \in \mathbb F_q\}$ be the axis-parallel line which passes through~$\boldsymbol{u}$ in the $\boldsymbol{i}$-th direction.
nodes.statement_short: Sample role, point and axis direction

nodes.name: Query the line player for a degree-d polynomial
nodes.statement: Player~$\boldsymbol{r}$: Give $\boldsymbol{\ell}$; receive the univariate degree-$d$ polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{\ell} \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Query the line player for a degree-d polynomial

nodes.name: Query the other player at the point
nodes.statement: Player~$\overline{\boldsymbol{r}}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Query the other player at the point

nodes.name: Accept iff the line polynomial agrees with the point answer
nodes.statement: Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: Accept iff the line polynomial agrees with the point answer

nodes.name: Self-consistency test
nodes.statement: \textbf{Self-consistency test:} Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. \begin{itemize} \item[$\circ$] Player~$\mathrm{A}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$. \item[$\circ$] Player~$\mathrm{B}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb F_q$. \end{itemize} Accept if $\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{b}$.

nodes.name: Sample a random point
nodes.statement: \textbf{Self-consistency test:} Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point.

nodes.name: Query Player A at the point
nodes.statement: Player~$\mathrm{A}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Query Player A at the point

nodes.name: Query Player B at the point
nodes.statement: Player~$\mathrm{B}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Query Player B at the point

nodes.name: Accept iff answers agree
nodes.statement: Accept if $\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{b}$.

nodes.name: Diagonal lines test
nodes.statement: \textbf{Diagonal lines test:} Pick a uniformly random role $\boldsymbol{r} \sim \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. Select $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$ uniformly at random, and let $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point whose last $m - \boldsymbol{i}$ coordinates are~$0$. Finally, let $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \{\boldsymbol{u} + t \cdot \boldsymbol{v} \mid t \in \mathbb F_q\}$ be the line which passes through~$\boldsymbol{u}$ in direction~$\boldsymbol{v}$. \begin{itemize} \item[$\circ$] Player~$\boldsymbol{r}$: Give $\boldsymbol{\ell}$; receive the univariate degree-$md$ polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{\ell} \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$. \item[$\circ$] Player~$\overline{\boldsymbol{r}}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$. \end{itemize} Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$.

nodes.name: Sample role, point, index and direction vector
nodes.statement: \textbf{Diagonal lines test:} Pick a uniformly random role $\boldsymbol{r} \sim \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Let $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point. Select $\boldsymbol{i} \sim \{1, \ldots, m\}$ uniformly at random, and let $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb F_q^m$ be a uniformly random point whose last $m - \boldsymbol{i}$ coordinates are~$0$. Finally, let $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \{\boldsymbol{u} + t \cdot \boldsymbol{v} \mid t \in \mathbb F_q\}$ be the line which passes through~$\boldsymbol{u}$ in direction~$\boldsymbol{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sample role, point, index and direction vector

nodes.name: Query the line player for a degree-md polynomial
nodes.statement: Player~$\boldsymbol{r}$: Give $\boldsymbol{\ell}$; receive the univariate degree-$md$ polynomial $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{\ell} \rightarrow \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Query the line player for a degree-md polynomial

nodes.name: Query the other player at the point
nodes.statement: Player~$\overline{\boldsymbol{r}}$: Give $\boldsymbol{u}$; receive $\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathbb F_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Query the other player at the point

nodes.name: Accept iff the line polynomial agrees with the point answer
nodes.statement: Accept if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: Accept iff the line polynomial agrees with the point answer

nodes.name: Case a = 0: the sum is 1
nodes.statement: If $a = 0$, then $\mathrm{tr}[x \cdot a] = 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb F_q$. As a result, \begin{equation*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[{\boldsymbol{x}} \cdot a]} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q} \omega^{0} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q} 1 = 1. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Case a nonzero: shift invariance forces C = 0
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, if $a 
eq 0$, then there exists a $y \in \mathbb F_q$ such that $\mathrm{tr}[a \cdot y] 
eq 0$. As a result,  egin{equation*} C := \mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[{ oldsymbol{x}} \cdot a]} = \mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q} \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[({ oldsymbol{x}}+y) \cdot a]} = \mathop{ f E/}_{{ oldsymbol{x}} \sim \mathbb F_q} (\omega^{\mathrm{tr}[{ oldsymbol{x}} \cdot a]} \cdot \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[y \cdot a]}) = C \cdot \omega^{\mathrm{tr}[y\cdot a]}. \end{equation*} But because $\mathrm{tr}[y \cdot a] 
eq 0$, $\omega^{\mathrm{tr}[y\cdot a]} 
eq 1$. This implies that $C = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Case a nonzero: shift invariance forces C = 0

nodes.name: Rewrite the A-C inconsistency
nodes.statement: First, we can rewrite the consistency between $A$ and $C$ as \begin{align*} \delta \geq \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a \neq b} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi} & = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes (C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}} - C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \\ & = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \\ & = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \bra{\psi} I \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$A$ is a measurement}\\ & = \bra{\psi} I \otimes C \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Rewrite the B-C inconsistency similarly
nodes.statement: Likewise, we can rewrite the inconsistency between $B$ and $C$ as \begin{align*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a \neq b} \bra{\psi} B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi} &= \bra{\psi} I \otimes C \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Reduce to comparing the two inconsistencies
nodes.statement: We want to show that the inconsistency between~$B$ and~$C$ is close to the inconsistency between $A$ and $B$. In particular, we claim that \begin{equation*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a \neq b} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi} \approx_{\sqrt{\epsilon}} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a \neq b} \bra{\psi} B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to comparing the two inconsistencies

nodes.name: Bound the difference by Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference using Cauchy-Schwarz. \begin{align*} & \Big| \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a } \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \otimes C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a\ket{\psi} \Big| \nonumber \\ \leq~& \sqrt{ \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} I \otimes (C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi}} \\ \leq~& \sqrt{\epsilon} \cdot 1. \tag{because~$C$ is a sub-measurement} \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Expand and bound the squared distance by 2 delta
nodes.statement: Our goal is to bound \begin{align*} &\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a\Vert (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \Vert^2\\ =~&\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi}\\ =~&\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} +\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} I \otimes (B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi} - 2 \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}\\ \leq~&\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} +\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} I \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} - 2 \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}\\ =~&2 - 2 \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$A$ and~$B$ are measurements}\\ \leq~& 2 - 2 \cdot(1-\delta) \tag{by~\Cref{prop:simeq-for-measurements} and the fact that~$A$ and~$B$ are measurements}\\ =~&2 \delta. \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand and bound the squared distance by 2 delta

nodes.name: Projective case gives equality, hence iff
nodes.statement: When $A$ and~$B$ are projective, ``if and only if'' follows from the first inequality becoming an equality.
nodes.statement_short: Projective case gives equality, hence iff

nodes.name: Prove the first statement via Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: We begin by showing~\Cref{eq:closeness3}. \begin{align*} &\Big | \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a,b} \bra{\psi} C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a,b} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \Big | \\ &= \Big | \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} \Big ( \sum_b C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a,b} \Big ) \cdot (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \Big |\\ &\leq \Big ( \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Big(\sum_b C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a,b}\Big) \Big(\sum_b C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a,b}\Big)^\dagger \ket{\psi} \Big )^{1/2} \cdot \Big ( \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^\dagger (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2} \\ &\leq \sqrt{\gamma}. \end{align*} The third line uses Cauchy-Schwarz, and the fourth line uses the assumption $\sum_a (\sum_b C^x_{a,b}) (\sum_b C^x_{a,b})^\dagger \leq I$ to bound the first factor by $1$ and the assumption $A^x_a \approx_\gamma B^x_a$ to bound the second factor by $\sqrt{\gamma}$.
nodes.section: 4.4.3 Deriving consistency relations from the state-dependent distance
nodes.statement_short: Prove the first statement via Cauchy-Schwarz

nodes.name: Reduce the second statement to the first by adjoints
nodes.statement: As for \Cref{eq:closeness4}, we want to bound \begin{equation*} \Big | \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a,b} \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a,b} \ket{\psi} \Big | = \Big | \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a,b} \bra{\psi} (C^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a,b})^\dagger ((A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^\dagger - (B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^\dagger) \ket{\psi} \Big |. \end{equation*} It then follows from \Cref{eq:closeness3} that this is at most $\sqrt{\gamma}$.
nodes.section: 4.4.3 Deriving consistency relations from the state-dependent distance
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the second statement to the first by adjoints

nodes.name: Convert consistencies to closeness
nodes.statement: Because $B$, $C$, and~$D$ are measurements, \Cref{prop:simeq-to-approx} implies that \begin{equation*} C^x_a \otimes I \approx_{2\delta} I \otimes B^x_a, \quad C^x_a \otimes I \approx_{2\gamma} I \otimes D^x_a. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Chain closeness by the triangle inequality
nodes.statement: The triangle inequality, \Cref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-approx_delta}, then implies that \begin{equation*} I \otimes B^x_a \approx_{4 \delta + 4 \gamma} I \otimes D^x_a. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain closeness by the triangle inequality

nodes.name: Transfer consistency to D
nodes.statement: Finally, \Cref{prop:triangle-sub} implies that \begin{equation*} A^x_a \otimes I \simeq_{\epsilon + \sqrt{4 \delta + 4 \gamma}} I \otimes D^x_a. \end{equation*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Bound the first approximation by the inconsistency
nodes.statement: We establish the first approximation in \Cref{eq:closeness5}: \begin{align*} &\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Big (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes (I - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \Big)^2 \ket{\psi} \\ &\leq \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes (I - B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \\ &= \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{\substack{a,b : \\ b \neq a}} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi} \\ &\leq \gamma \,. \end{align*} The first inequality folows from the fact that $A^x_a \otimes (I - B^x_a)$ has operator norm at most $1$, and the third line follows from the fact that $\{B^x_b\}$ is a complete measurement, and the last line follows from the assumption of consistency between the $A$ and $B$ (sub-)measurements.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the first approximation by the inconsistency

nodes.name: Bound the second approximation similarly
nodes.statement: To establish the second approximation in \Cref{eq:closeness5}, we compute the difference: \begin{align*} &\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Big ( (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}} - A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \Big)^2 \ket{\psi} \\ &\leq \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}} - A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \\ &= \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{\substack{a,a' : \\ a \neq a'}} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a'} \otimes B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \\ &\leq \gamma \,. \end{align*} The second line follows from the fact that $(A^x - A^x_a) \otimes B^x_a$ has operator norm at most $1$, and the last inequality follows from the consistency between the $A$ and $B$ (sub-)measurements.

nodes.name: Plan: prove first approximation in two steps
nodes.statement: We will show the first approximation in \Cref{eq:switch-sandwich} in two steps.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: prove first approximation in two steps

nodes.name: Shift the right A across the tensor product
nodes.statement: First, we show that \begin{equation} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a B A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{\sqrt{\delta}} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a B \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To do so, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big| \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a B \otimes I)\cdot (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi} \Big|\\ \leq~& \Big( \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a B^2 A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2} \cdot \Big(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2} \\ \leq~& \sqrt{\delta}.\tag{because $B \leq I$ and \eqref{eq:Aapproxd}} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Shift the right A across the tensor product

nodes.name: Shift the left A across, using projectivity
nodes.statement: Next, we show that \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:shift-right-A} = \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a B \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \approx_{\sqrt{\delta}} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_ a\bra{\psi} B \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*} To do so, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \cdot(B \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi}\Big| \tag{because~$A$ is projective}\\ \leq~& \Big( \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2} \cdot \Big(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} B^2 \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2} \\ \leq~& \sqrt{\delta}.\tag{because $B \leq I$ and \eqref{eq:Aapproxd}} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Shift the left A across, using projectivity

nodes.name: First approximation follows
nodes.statement: Thus, the first approximation in \Cref{eq:switch-sandwich} follows.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz for the second approximation
nodes.statement: To show the second approximation, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} (B\otimes I) \cdot ( A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a ) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ =~&\Big|\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \bra{\psi} (B\otimes I)\cdot \sum_a ( A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a ) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~& \Big( \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \bra{\psi} B^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2} \cdot \Big( \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a,b} \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \cdot(A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b) \ket{\psi} \Big)^{1/2}. \end{align*} The first term in the product is at most $1$ because $B \leq I$.

nodes.name: Bound the remaining square root by delta
nodes.statement: We bound the expression inside the second square root as follows. \begin{align*} &\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a,b} \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \cdot(A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b) \ket{\psi} \\ =~&\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a, b} \bra{\psi}(A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \otimes I + I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b - A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b - A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)\ket{\psi}\\ =~& \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} I \otimes (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi} - 2\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a,b} \bra{\psi}A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$A$ is projective} \\ \leq~& \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} I \otimes (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi} - 2\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi}A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} \\ =~& \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \\ \leq~& \delta, \end{align*} where the last step uses \Cref{eq:Aapproxd}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the remaining square root by delta

nodes.name: Bound disagreement by completeness minus agreement
nodes.statement: For a sub-measurement~$A$, \begin{align*} &\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a \neq b} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_b \ket{\psi}\\ =~& \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}- A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi}\\ \leq~&\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes (I- A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi}\\ =~&\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}\\ =~& \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi}. \end{align*} This is at most~$\delta$ if $A$ is $\delta$-strongly self-consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Bound disagreement by completeness minus agreement

nodes.name: Equality for measurements gives the converse
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if~$A$ is a measurement, then the inequality becomes an equality. Hence, if $A^x_a \otimes I \simeq_{\delta} I \otimes A^x_a$, then $A$ is $\delta$-strongly self-consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Equality for measurements gives the converse

nodes.name: Expand and bound the squared distance
nodes.statement_short: Expand and bound the squared distance

nodes.name: Projective case: equality gives the converse
nodes.statement: If~$A$ is projective, then \Cref{eq:here's-where-projectivity-would-help} becomes an equality, and so $A^x_a \otimes I \approx_{2\delta} I \otimes A^x_a$ implies that \begin{equation*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_a \Vert(A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a \otimes I - I \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_a) \ket{\psi}\Vert^2\right) \leq \delta.\qedhere \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Projective case: equality gives the converse

nodes.name: Expand the squared distance
Lower bound the post-processed agreement
nodes.statement: The second term in \Cref{eq:finishing-this-up} can be bounded by \begin{align*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_b \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{[f(a)=b]} \ket{\psi} &= \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a, a': f(a) = f(a')} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a'} \ket{\psi}\\ &\geq\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \ket{\psi}\\ &\geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\delta. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Combine to get 2 delta
nodes.statement: Hence, \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:finishing-this-up} \leq 2\cdot \Big( \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - (\bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\delta)\Big) = 2\delta. \end{equation*} This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Claim: P post-processed is close to A on the other side
nodes.statement_short: Claim: P post-processed is close to A on the other side

nodes.name: Expand the squared distance into three terms
nodes.statement_short: Expand the squared distance into three terms

nodes.name: Bound the first term by completeness transfer
nodes.statement: By \Cref{prop:completeness-transfer-projective-P}, the first term in \Cref{eq:gonna-handle-third-term} is at most \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} P \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} + 2\sqrt{\epsilon}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the first term by completeness transfer

nodes.name: Lower bound the cross term
nodes.statement: As for the third term in \Cref{eq:gonna-handle-third-term}, we can bound it by \begin{align*} \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_b \bra{\psi} P^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{[f(a)=b]} \ket{\psi} &= \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a, a': f(a) = f(a')} \bra{\psi} P^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a'} \ket{\psi}\\ &\geq \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} P^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \ket{\psi}\\ &\geq \mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \otimes A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}}_{a} \ket{\psi} - \sqrt{\epsilon} \tag{by \Cref{prop:easy-approx-from-approx-delta}} \\ &\geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \delta - \sqrt{\epsilon}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Combine to prove the claim
nodes.statement: Putting everything together, \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:gonna-handle-third-term} \leq (\bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} + 2\sqrt{\epsilon}) + \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 2 \cdot(\bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \delta - \sqrt{\epsilon}) = 2\delta + 4\sqrt{\epsilon}. \end{equation*} This proves \Cref{eq;what-we-want-to-prove-but-on-wrong-side}.

nodes.name: Self-closeness of post-processed A
nodes.statement: \Cref{prop:two-notions-of-self-consistency-after-evaluation} implies that \begin{equation*} A^x_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes I \approx_{2\delta} I \otimes A^x_{[f(a)=b]}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Chain the two closeness statements
nodes.statement: Hence, by \Cref{eq;what-we-want-to-prove-but-on-wrong-side}, \begin{equation*} P^x_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes I \approx_{2\delta + 4\sqrt{\epsilon}} I \otimes A_{[f(a)=b]}^x \approx_{2\delta} A^x_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes I. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Apply the triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Thus, by \Cref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-approx_delta}, \begin{equation*} P^x_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes I \approx_{8\delta + 8\sqrt{\epsilon}}A^x_{[f(a)=b]} \otimes I. \end{equation*} This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz upper bound on the agreement
nodes.statement: Applying Cauchy-Schwarz, we have \begin{align} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_a \ket{\psi} &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a \otimes I) \cdot (I \otimes A_a) \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ &\leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} I \otimes (A_a)^2 \ket{\psi}}\nonumber\\ & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz upper bound on the agreement

nodes.name: Combine with self-consistency
nodes.statement: As a result, \begin{align*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} &\geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_a \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{eq:As-on-same-side-rewrite}}\\ &\geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\zeta. \tag{by self-consistency of~$A$} \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Split the distance into B-closeness and incomplete part
nodes.statement:
By \Cref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-vectors-squared} (the triangle inequality for vectors squared),  egin{align*} &\phantom{=}\sum_a \Vert(A_a - C_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2\ & = \sum_{a 
eq a^*} \Vert(A_a - B_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 + \Vert(A_{a^*} - (I-B + B_{a^*}))\otimes I\ket{\psi}\Vert^2\ & \leq \sum_{a 
eq a^*} \Vert(A_a - B_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 + 2 \cdot \Vert(A_{a^*} - B_{a^*})\otimes I\ket{\psi}\Vert^2 + 2 \cdot \Vert(I - B) \otimes I\ket{\psi}\Vert^2\ & \leq 2\sum_{a 
eq a^*} \Vert(A_a - B_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 + 2 \cdot \Vert(A_{a^*} - B_{a^*})\otimes I\ket{\psi}\Vert^2 + 2 \cdot \Vert(I - B) \otimes I\ket{\psi}\Vert^2\ & = 2\sum_{a} \Vert(A_a - B_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 + 2 \cdot \Vert(I - B)\otimes I \ket{\psi}\Vert^2\ & \leq 2 \delta + 2 \cdot \Vert(I - B)\otimes I \ket{\psi}\Vert^2. 	ag{because $A_a \otimes I \approx_{\delta} B_a \otimes I$} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split the distance into B-closeness and incomplete part

nodes.name: Bound the incomplete part by 1 minus squared weight of B
nodes.statement_short: Bound the incomplete part by 1 minus squared weight of B

nodes.name: Lower bound squared weight of B via A
nodes.statement: Now, by \Cref{prop:easy-approx-from-approx-delta} and the fact that $A_a\otimes I \approx_{\delta} B_a\otimes I$, \begin{align*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} B_a^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} & \approx_{\sqrt{\delta}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a \cdot B_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ & \approx_{\sqrt{\delta}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a^2\otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ & \geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi}- \zeta \tag{by \Cref{prop:cool-prop}}\\ & = 1 - \zeta. \tag{because~$A$ is a measurement} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound squared weight of B via A

nodes.name: Combine the bounds
nodes.statement: Hence, by \Cref{eq:to-return-later-whatevs}, \begin{equation*} \Vert(I - B) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Vert^2 \leq 1 -\sum_a \bra{\psi} B_a^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 2\sqrt{\delta} + \zeta. \end{equation*} This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Fix a basis of C^{k+1}
nodes.statement: We will consider an orthonormal basis for $\mathbb C^{k+1}$ consisting of a vector $\ket{a}$ for each $a \in \mathcal{A}$ and the vector $\ket{\bot}$.

nodes.name: Choose the dilating unitary U
nodes.statement: Let~$U$ be any unitary such that for each vector $\ket{\psi} \in \mathbb C^d$, \begin{align*} U \cdot (\ket{\psi} \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}) &= \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} ((A_{a})^{1/2} \ket{\psi}) \otimes \ket{a} + ((1 - A)^{1/2}\ket{\psi}) \otimes \ket{\bot}\\ &= \Big(\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} (A_{a})^{1/2} \otimes \ket{a} + (1 - A)^{1/2} \otimes \ket{\bot}\Big) \cdot \ket{\psi}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Express U on the auxiliary state
nodes.statement: This implies that \begin{equation*} U \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} (A_{a})^{1/2} \otimes \ket{a} + (1 - A)^{1/2} \otimes \ket{\bot}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Express U on the auxiliary state

nodes.name: Project onto |a> to get sqrt(A_a)
nodes.statement: Hence, for any $a \in \mathcal{A}$, \begin{equation*} (I \otimes \bra{a}) \cdot U \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}) = (I \otimes \bra{a}) \cdot \Big(\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} (A_{a})^{1/2} \otimes \ket{a} + (1 - A)^{1/2} \otimes \ket{\bot}\Big) = (A_a)^{1/2}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Define the projective sub-measurement
nodes.statement: Then the desired projective sub-measurement is \[ \widehat{A}_a = U^{\dagger} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{a} \bra{a}) \cdot U. \]

nodes.name: Verify the compression equals A_a
nodes.statement: This is because \begin{align*} (I \otimes \bra{\mathsf{aux}} ) \cdot \widehat{A}_{a} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}) &=(I \otimes \bra{\mathsf{aux}} ) \cdot (U^{\dagger} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{a} \bra{a}) \cdot U) \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}})\\ &=(I \otimes \bra{\mathsf{aux}} ) \cdot U^{\dagger} \cdot (I \otimes \ket{a}) \cdot (I\otimes \bra{a}) \cdot U \cdot (I \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}})\\ &= (A_a)^{1/2} \cdot (A_a)^{1/2} = A_a. \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Dilate each question with its own auxiliary register
nodes.statement: For each $x$, let $k$ be the number of outcomes in $A^x$, and let $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A},x}}$ be a state of dimensionality $k+1$. Let $\widetilde{A}^x$ be the sub-measurement guaranteed by \Cref{lem:naimark-helper}. Define $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B},x}}$ and $\widetilde{B}^x$ similarly. We define \begin{equation*} \ket{\widehat{\psi}} = \ket{\psi} \otimes \big(\otimes_{x} \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A},x}}\big) \otimes \big(\otimes_{x} \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B},x}}\big) \end{equation*} and \begin{align*} \widehat{A}^x_a &= \widetilde{A}^x_a \otimes \big(\otimes_{z \neq x} I_{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A},z}}\big)\\ \widehat{B}^y_b &= \widetilde{B}^y_b \otimes \big(\otimes_{z\neq y} I_{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B},z}}\big). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Dilate each question with its own auxiliary register

nodes.name: Verify outcome statistics are preserved
nodes.statement: Then for all $x,y,z,b$, \begin{align*} \bra{\widehat{\psi}} \widehat{A}^x_a \otimes \widehat{B}^y_b \ket{\widehat{\psi}} & = \bra{\psi} \otimes \bra{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A},x}} \otimes \bra{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B},y}} \cdot \widetilde{A}^x_a \otimes \widetilde{B}^y_b \cdot \ket{\psi} \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A},x}} \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B},y}}\\ &= \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^y_b \ket{\psi}. \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Assume strong self-consistency of A
nodes.statement: Let $A = \{A_a\}$ be a sub-measurement with outcomes $a \in \mathcal{A}$ whose strong self-consistency is \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_a \ket{\psi} \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\zeta. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Lower bound <A tensor A>
nodes.statement: Note that \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} A \otimes A \ket{\psi} = \sum_{a, b} \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_b \ket{\psi} \geq \sum_{a} \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_a \ket{\psi} \geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\zeta. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Bound <A tensor (I-A)> by zeta
nodes.statement: Rearranging, \begin{align*} \bra{\psi} A \otimes (I - A)\ket{\psi} &= \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \bra{\psi} A \otimes A \ket{\psi}\\ &\leq (\bra{\psi} A \otimes A \ket{\psi} + \zeta) - \bra{\psi} A \otimes A \ket{\psi} = \zeta. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Lower bound <(I-A) tensor (I-A)>
nodes.statement: As a result, \begin{align*} \bra{\psi} (I-A) \otimes (I-A) \ket{\psi} &= \bra{\psi} (I-A) \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \bra{\psi} (I-A) \otimes A \ket{\psi}\\ &\geq \bra{\psi} (I-A) \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \zeta. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Complete A with a bot outcome
nodes.statement: Let $\widehat{A}$ be the POVM measurement with outcomes in $\widehat{\mathcal{A}} = \mathcal{A} \cup \{\bot\}$ defined as \begin{equation*} \widehat{A}_a = \left\{\begin{array}{cl} A_a & \text{if $a \in \mathcal{A}$},\\ (I-A) & \text{if $a = \bot$.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Complete A with a bot outcome

nodes.name: Completion has self-consistency 1-2zeta
nodes.statement: Then the strong self-consistency of $\widehat{A}$ is \begin{align*} \sum_{a \in \widehat{\mathcal{A}}} \bra{\psi} \widehat{A}_a \otimes \widehat{A}_a \ket{\psi} & = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_a \ket{\psi} + \bra{\psi} \widehat{A}_{\bot} \otimes \widehat{A}_{\bot} \ket{\psi}\\ & \geq \Big(\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \zeta\Big) + \bra{\psi} (I-A) \otimes (I-A) \ket{\psi}\\ & \geq \Big( \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \zeta\Big) + \Big(\bra{\psi} (I-A) \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \zeta\Big)\\ & = 1 - 2\zeta. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Convert to consistency via Prop 4.35
nodes.statement: Because $\widehat{A}$ is a measurement, \Cref{prop:other-two-notions-of-self-consistency} states that this is equivalent to \begin{equation*} \widehat{A}_a \otimes I \simeq_{2\zeta} I \otimes \widehat{A}_a. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Apply the measurement orthogonalization lemma
nodes.statement: As a result, \Cref{lem:orthonormalization-main-lemma} implies the existence of a projective sub-measurement $\widehat{P} = \{\widehat{P}_a\}_{a \in \widehat{\mathcal{A}}}$ such that \begin{equation*} \widehat{A}_a \otimes I \approx_{84\cdot(2\zeta)^{1/4}} \widehat{P}_a \otimes I. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Restrict the projective sub-measurement to original outcomes
nodes.statement: If we define the projective sub-measurement $P = \{P_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ by $P_a = \widehat{P}_a$ for all $a \in \mathcal{A}$, then \begin{equation*} \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \Vert (A_a - P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 \leq \sum_{a \in \widehat{\mathcal{A}}} \Vert (\widehat{A}_a - \widehat{P}_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 \leq 84 \cdot (2\zeta)^{1/4}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the projective sub-measurement to original outcomes

nodes.name: Conclude with constant 100
nodes.statement: Thus, $A_a \otimes I \approx_{84 \cdot (2\zeta)^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I$. We conclude the proof by noting that $84 \cdot (2\zeta)^{1/4} \leq 100 \cdot \zeta^{1/4}$ because $84 \cdot (2)^{1/4} \approx 99.89\leq100$.

nodes.name: WLOG zeta <= 1/4
nodes.statement: We note that the lemma as stated is trivial when $\zeta > 1/4$. As a result, we will assume that \begin{equation} \zeta \leq 1/4. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Fix measurements A,B with consistency zeta
nodes.statement: Let $A = \{A_a\}$ and~$B = \{B_a\}$ be POVM measurements such that \begin{equation*} A_a \otimes I \simeq_{\zeta} I \otimes B_a. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Fix measurements A,B with consistency zeta

nodes.name: Agreement at least 1-zeta
nodes.statement: By \Cref{prop:simeq-for-measurements}, this implies that \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi}A_a \otimes B_a \ket{\psi} \geq 1 - \zeta. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz bound on the agreement
nodes.statement: Applying Cauchy-Schwarz, we have \begin{align*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes B_a \ket{\psi} &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a \otimes I) \cdot (I \otimes B_a) \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ &\leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} I \otimes (B_a)^2 \ket{\psi}}\nonumber\\ & \leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot 1. \end{align*}

nodes.name: A is nearly projective: sum (A_a - A_a^2) <= 2zeta
nodes.statement: Taking the square of both sides, \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq \Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes B_a \ket{\psi}\Big)^2 \geq (1-\zeta)^2 \geq 1 - 2\zeta = \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 2\zeta. \tag{because~$A$ is a measurement} \end{equation*} Rearranging, \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - (A_a)^2) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 2\zeta. \end{equation} This is all we need the~$B$ measurement for; henceforth, we will derive consequences of~\Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}.
nodes.statement_short: A is nearly projective: sum (A_a - A_a^2) <= 2zeta

nodes.name: Rounding lemma for A
nodes.statement: In our next lemma, we convert each~$A_a$ to a projective matrix~$R_a$ by rounding each of $A_a$'s large eigenvalues to~$1$ and small eigenvalues to~$0$. \begin{lemma}[Rounding to projectors] There exists a set of projective matrices $\{R_a\}$ such that \begin{equation*} A_a \otimes I \approx_{2\sqrt{\zeta}} R_a \otimes I. \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} R:= \sum_a R_a \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} For each~$a$, we write the eigendecomposition of $A_a$ as follows: \begin{equation*} A_a = \sum_i \lambda_{a, i} \cdot\ket{u_{a, i}} \bra{u_{a, i}}. \end{equation*} Let \begin{equation} 0 < \delta \leq 1/2 \end{equation} be a number to be decided later. Let $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta:[0, 1] \rightarrow \{0, 1\}$ be the truncation function defined as \begin{equation*} \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{rl} 1 & \text{if } x \geq 1- \delta,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} Then for each~$a$ we define the matrix $R_a$ \begin{equation*} R_a = \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a) = \sum_i \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(\lambda_{a, i}) \cdot \ket{u_{a, i}} \bra{u_{a, i}}. \end{equation*} To analyze this, we will require the following technical lemma. \begin{lemma} For any $x \in [0, 1]$, \begin{equation*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} This is proved by case analysis. First, suppose that $x \geq 1 - \delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 1$. In addition, because $\delta \leq 1/2$ by \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}, $ x \geq 1 - \delta \geq 1/2 \geq \delta. $ Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = (1-x)^2\\ &\leq (1-x)\\ &\leq (1-x) \cdot \frac{x}{\delta} \tag{because $x \geq \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} Next, suppose that $x < 1 -\delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 0$. Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = x^2\\ &\leq x\\ &\leq x \cdot \frac{(1-x)}{\delta} \tag{because $x \leq 1- \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} This concludes the proof. \end{proof} As a result, for each~$a$, \Cref{lem:trunc-inequality} implies that \begin{equation*} (A_a - R_a)^2 = (A_a - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (A_a - (A_a)^2). \end{equation*} Thus, \begin{align*} \sum_a \Vert (A_a - R_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Vert^2 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - R_a)^2 \otimes I\ket{\psi} &\leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - (A_a)^2) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &\leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot 2\zeta. \tag{by \Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}} \end{align*} This implies that $A_a \otimes I \approx_{2\zeta/\delta} R_a \otimes I$. Next, for each $x \in [0, 1]$, it follows from the definition of $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta$ that \begin{equation*} \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot x. \end{equation*} Thus, for each~$a$ \begin{equation*} R_a = \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a) \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot A_a. \end{equation*} Summing over all~$a$, \begin{equation*} R = \sum_a R_a \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot \sum_a A_a = \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot A = \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot I, \end{equation*} because~$A$ is a measurement. We note that \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{1-\delta} = \frac{1}{1-\delta} \cdot \frac{1 + 2\delta}{1 + 2\delta} = \frac{1 + 2\delta}{1 + \delta - 2\delta^2} \leq 1 + 2\delta, \end{equation*} because \begin{equation*} 1 + \delta - 2\delta^2 = 1 + \delta\cdot(1-2\delta)\geq 1 \end{equation*} when $\delta \leq 1/2$, which we assumed in \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}. Hence, \begin{equation*} R \leq (1+ 2\delta) \cdot I. \end{equation*} The lemma now follows by setting $\delta = \sqrt{\zeta}$. Note that we required that $\delta$ be at most $1/2$, which follows from our assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Rank reduction lemma
Completeness of Q
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we let $Q = \{Q_a\}$ be the set of projective matrices given by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}. We now derive a few properties of~$Q$ that follow as a consequence of \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}. To begin, we show that~$Q$ is almost as complete as~$A$. \begin{lemma}[Completeness of~$Q$] \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} To begin, we claim that \begin{align} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{because the $Q_a$'s are projective}\\ & \approx_{5 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{align} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \otimes I) \cdot ((Q_a - A_a) \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~&\sqrt{\sum_a\bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{1+2\sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot \sqrt{12\sqrt{\zeta}} \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{12\sqrt{\zeta}}, \end{align*} where the last line uses the assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}. Next, we claim that \begin{equation} \eqref{eq:Q-for-an-A} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{4 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((Q_a - A_a) \otimes I) \cdot (A_a \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~&\sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a\bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{12 \sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot 1. \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}} \end{align*} In conclusion, \begin{align*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 9 \zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:Q-for-an-A,eq:another-Q-for-A}}\\ & \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 2\zeta - 9\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}}\\ & \geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 11 \zeta^{1/4} \nonumber\\ & = 1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Completeness of sqrt(Q)
Q is almost projective
nodes.statement: Finally, we show the following lemma, which quantifies a sense in which~$Q$ is ``almost projective". \begin{lemma}[$Q$ is almost projective] \begin{equation*} \sum_a (Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a) \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot I. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum} implies that $Q \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I$. As a result, \begin{align*} &\sum_a Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - \sum_a Q_a\\ \leq ~&(1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \sum_a Q_a \cdot I \cdot Q_a - \sum_a Q_a \\ = ~&(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \sum_a Q_a - \sum_a Q_a \tag{because the $Q_a$'s are projectors}\\ = ~&(1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot Q - Q\\ = ~& 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot Q\\ \leq~& 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I\\ \leq~& 2 \sqrt{\zeta} \cdot 2 \cdot I. \tag{by \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}} \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Matrix decomposition of Q_a
nodes.statement: We now arrive at the most important definition in this proof, which is a natural matrix decomposition for the $Q_a$ matrices. \begin{definition}[Matrix decomposition of~$Q_a$] For each $a$, let $m_a$ be the rank of $Q_a$. Let $\ket{v_{a, 1}}, \ldots, \ket{v_{a, m_a}}$ be an orthonormal basis for the range of $Q_a$, so that \begin{equation*} Q_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}. \end{equation*} Let $m = \sum_a m_a$, and consider an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^m$ consisting of vectors $\ket{a, i}$ for each $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$. For each $a$, define the matrix \begin{equation*} X_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{v_{a, i}}. \end{equation*} In addition, define the matrix \begin{equation} X = \sum_a X_a = \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{v_{a, i}}. \end{equation} Finally, we let $T = \{T_a\}$ be the projective measurement on $\mathbb C^m$ defined as \begin{equation*} T_a = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i}\bra{a, i}. \end{equation*} \end{definition}

nodes.name: Basic properties of X_a
nodes.statement: The next pair of lemmas will prove some basic properties of the~$X_a$ matrices. \begin{lemma} For each~$a$, $\displaystyle X_a = T_a \cdot X. $ \end{lemma} \begin{proof} This is a simple calculation: \begin{equation*} T_a \cdot X = \Big(\sum_i^{m_a} \ket{a, i} \bra{a,i}\Big)\cdot \Big( \sum_a \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i}\bra{v_{a, i}}\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{a, i}\bra{v_{a, i}} = X_a.\qedhere \end{equation*} \end{proof} \begin{lemma}[$Q_a$ restated] For each~$a$, \begin{equation*} Q_a = X^\dagger_a \cdot X_a = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} The first equality follows from \begin{align*} X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a &= \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{a, i} \Big) \cdot \Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, j}}\bra{a, j} \Big)^\dagger\nonumber\\ &= \sum_{i, j=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{a, i} \cdot \ket{a, j} \bra{v_{a, j}} = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}} = Q_a. \end{align*} The remaining equalities follow from \Cref{lem:xa-t} and the fact that~$T$ is a projective measurement. \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = (X^\dagger \cdot T_a) \cdot (T_a \cdot X) = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X.\qedhere \end{equation*} \end{proof}

nodes.name: SVD of X and notation
nodes.statement: Now we introduce our main tool for studying~$X$, which is via its singular value decomposition. \begin{definition}[SVD of~$X$] Let $X = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger$ be the singular value decomposition (SVD) of~$X$. Because~$X$ is an $m \times d$ matrix, the definition of the SVD states that $U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary matrix, $V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary matrix, and $\Sigma_{m\times d}$ is an $m \times d$ diagonal matrix with nonnegative real numbers on its diagonal. \end{definition} \begin{notation} For positive integers $h$ and~$w$, we will write $I_{h \times w}$ for the $h \times w$ matrix with $1$'s on its diagonal and $0$'s everywhere else. For integers $h, w \geq m$, we also write $\Sigma_{h \times w}$ for the $h \times w$ diagonal matrix whose diagonal agrees with $\Sigma_{m \times d}$'s; namely, $(\Sigma_{h \times w})_{i, i} = (\Sigma_{m \times d})_{i,i}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$ and $(\Sigma_{h \times w})_{i, i} = 0$ for all $i > m$. We note that because $\Sigma_{m \times d}$ is a real-valued diagonal matrix, $(\Sigma_{h \times w})^\dagger = \Sigma_{w \times h}$. \end{notation}

nodes.name: Square of X
nodes.statement: With this definition, we can give a helpful expression for the square of~$X$. \begin{lemma}[$X$ squared] \begin{equation*} X \cdot X^\dagger = U \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger, \quad \text{and} \quad X^\dagger \cdot X = Q = V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First, \begin{align*} X \cdot X^\dagger &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}. \end{align*} Second, \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot X & = \sum_a X^\dagger \cdot T_a X \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ &= \sum_a Q_a \tag{by \Cref{lem:qa-restated}}\\ &= Q. \end{align*} In addition, we can rewrite $X^\dagger \cdot X$ as \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot X &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\ &= V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger. \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Relate X expression to Q expression
nodes.statement: The following lemma relates an expression in the $X_a$'s with an expression in the~$Q_a$'s that appeared previously in \Cref{lem:q-almost-projective}. \begin{lemma} For each~$a$, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a = Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Using~\Cref{lem:X-squared} and~\Cref{lem:qa-restated}, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot Q \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a. \end{equation*} Similarly, because $Q_a$ is projective, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a = (X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot (X^\dagger \cdot X_a) = Q_a \cdot Q_a = Q_a. \end{equation*} Finally, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a. \end{equation*} Putting these together, \begin{align*} &X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a\\ =~& X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger - 2 \cdot X\cdot X^\dagger + I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a\\ =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - 2 \cdot Q_a + Q_a\\ =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a. \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Relate X expression to Q expression

nodes.name: Intuition and definition of P
nodes.statement: Now we are ready to state the projective sub-measurement~$P$ which should approximate~$A$. Before doing so, we give some intuition for the construction. \begin{remark} Suppose that the $Q_a$'s actually formed a projective measurement. This would imply that the vectors $\ket{v_{a, i}}$, over all $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$ form an orthonormal set. Then the SVD would actually have already been provided in \Cref{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition}; for each $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$, the corresponding singular value would be~$1$ and the corresponding left- and right-singular vectors would be $\ket{a, i}$ and $\ket{v_{a, i}}$, respectively. In particular, we would have $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$ and $X = U \cdot I_{m \times d}\cdot V^\dagger$. \end{remark} In reality, we don't know that $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$. However, we will construct~$P = \{P_a\}$ as if it were. This motivates the following definition. \begin{definition}[Definition of~$P$] Define the matrix \begin{equation*} \widehat{X} = U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger. \end{equation*} In addition, for each $a$, define the matrices \begin{equation*} \widehat{X}_a = T_a \cdot \widehat{X}, \quad P_a = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a. \end{equation*} \end{definition}

nodes.name: Properties of P and X-hat
nodes.statement: We now give analogues of \Cref{lem:qa-restated,lem:X-squared} for the~$P$ matrices. \begin{lemma}[$P_a$ restated] For each~$a$, \begin{equation*} P_a = \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} This follows from the definition of $\widehat{X}^\dagger_a$ and the fact that $T$ is a projective measurement: \begin{equation*} P_a = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a = (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a) \cdot (T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) = \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}.\qedhere \end{equation*} \end{proof} \begin{lemma}[$\widehat{X}$ squared] \begin{equation*} \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = I_{m \times m}. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First, \begin{align*} \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger &= (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}\\ &= I_{m \times m}, \end{align*} where the last step uses the fact that~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Lemmas mixing X and X-hat
nodes.statement: Finally, we show two lemmas on quantities involving both $X$ and~$\widehat{X}$. \begin{lemma}[$X$ times $\widehat{X}$] \begin{equation*} X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger, \quad \text{and} \quad X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} = \sqrt{Q}. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First, \begin{align*} X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}. \end{align*} Second, \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= \sqrt{V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger}\\ &= \sqrt{Q}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}} \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof} \begin{lemma}[Squared difference] \begin{equation*} (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \leq (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} By~\Cref{lem:X-squared,lem:X-hat-squared,lem:X-times-X-hat}, \begin{align*} (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger & = X \cdot X^\dagger - X\cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger - \widehat{X} \cdot X^\dagger + \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger\\ & = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - 2 \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger+ I_{m \times m}\\ & = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 - 2 \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m} \right) \cdot U^\dagger\\ & = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger. \end{align*} Because $\Sigma_{m \times m}$ and $I_{m \times m}$ are commuting, \begin{equation*} (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2 \leq (\Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2 = (\Sigma_{m\times m}^2 - I_{m \times m})^2. \end{equation*} As a result, \begin{align*} U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger & \leq U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger\\ & = \left(U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - I_{m \times m} \right)^2\\ &= (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}} \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: P is projective
nodes.statement: The first property we need of~$P$ is that it is a projective sub-measurement.
