This is shown in the following lemma. \begin{lemma}[Projectivity of~$P$] $P = \{P_a\}$ forms a projective sub-measurement. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $a, b$ be (possibly distinct) outcomes. Then \begin{align*} P_a \cdot P_b &= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \cdot (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X}) \tag{by \Cref{lem:pa-restated}}\\ &= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X}) \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\ &= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \cdot \boldsymbol{1}[a = b] \tag{because~$T$ is a projective measurement}\\ &= P_a \cdot \boldsymbol{1}[a=b]. \tag{by \Cref{lem:pa-restated}} \end{align*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: P is close to Q
nodes.statement: The second property we need of~$P$ is that it is close to~$A$. We will first show that it is close to~$Q$. \begin{lemma}[$P$ is close to~$Q$] \begin{equation*} Q_a \otimes I \approx_{30\zeta^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Our goal is to upper-bound the quantity \begin{align} &\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \bra{\psi} P\otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}, \end{align} where the last step uses the projectivity of~$Q$ and~$P$. We bound the four terms in \Cref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} separately. First, by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}, \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 1+2\sqrt{\zeta}. \end{equation*} Second, because~$P$ is a sub-measurement, \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} P \otimes I\ket{\psi} \leq 1. \end{equation*} The third term and fourth terms are significantly more complicated to bound. As they are complex conjugates of each other, we can write their sum as \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = 2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big). \end{equation} We now focus on the expression on the right-hand side of \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates}. To begin, we use \Cref{lem:qa-restated} to rewrite it as \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*} The main step will be to show that we can exchange the second $X$ for an $\widehat{X}$, i.e. \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{multline*} \Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X})) \otimes I) \cdot(P_a \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}. \end{multline*} The expression inside the first square root is \begin{align*} & \sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ \leq~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:squared-difference}}\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}}\\ \leq~& 4\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by~\Cref{lem:q-almost-projective}}\\ =~& 4\sqrt{\zeta}. \end{align*} The expression inside the second square root is at most~$1$ because~$P$ is a sub-measurement. Next, we claim that the \Cref{eq:add-a-hat} is in fact a real-valued expression. To see this, \begin{align*} \eqref{eq:add-a-hat} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:xa-t,lem:pa-restated}}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ &= \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-times-X-hat}}, \end{align*} which is real-valued because~$Q$ is positive semidefinite. As a result, we have \begin{align*} \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) & \geq \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) - 2\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:add-a-hat}}\\ & = \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi}- 2\zeta^{1/4}\\ & \geq (1 - 12 \zeta^{1/4}) - 2\zeta^{1/4}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:sqrt-Q-completeness}} \end{align*} In total, \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates} shows that \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 2 \cdot(1 - 14\zeta^{1/4}). \end{equation*} Putting everything together, we conclude that \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) + 1 - 2\cdot (1-14\zeta^{1/4}) = 2\sqrt{\zeta} + 28 \zeta^{1/4} \leq 30 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*} This completes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Chain A ~ Q ~ P by the triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Finally, we have that \begin{align*} A_a \otimes I &\approx_{12 \sqrt{\zeta}} Q_a \otimes I \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}}\\ &\approx_{30 \zeta^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I. \tag{by \Cref{lem:P-Q-approx}} \end{align*} Hence, \Cref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-approx_delta} implies that \begin{equation*} A_a \otimes I \approx_{84 \zeta^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I. \end{equation*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Chain A ~ Q ~ P by the triangle inequality

nodes.name: Eigendecompose A_a
nodes.statement: For each~$a$, we write the eigendecomposition of $A_a$ as follows: \begin{equation*} A_a = \sum_i \lambda_{a, i} \cdot\ket{u_{a, i}} \bra{u_{a, i}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Define truncation and R_a
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} 0 < \delta \leq 1/2 \end{equation} be a number to be decided later. Let $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta:[0, 1] \rightarrow \{0, 1\}$ be the truncation function defined as \begin{equation*} \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{rl} 1 & \text{if } x \geq 1- \delta,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} Then for each~$a$ we define the matrix $R_a$ \begin{equation*} R_a = \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a) = \sum_i \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(\lambda_{a, i}) \cdot \ket{u_{a, i}} \bra{u_{a, i}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Truncation inequality lemma
nodes.statement: To analyze this, we will require the following technical lemma. \begin{lemma} For any $x \in [0, 1]$, \begin{equation*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} This is proved by case analysis. First, suppose that $x \geq 1 - \delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 1$. In addition, because $\delta \leq 1/2$ by \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}, $ x \geq 1 - \delta \geq 1/2 \geq \delta. $ Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = (1-x)^2\\ &\leq (1-x)\\ &\leq (1-x) \cdot \frac{x}{\delta} \tag{because $x \geq \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} Next, suppose that $x < 1 -\delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 0$. Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = x^2\\ &\leq x\\ &\leq x \cdot \frac{(1-x)}{\delta} \tag{because $x \leq 1- \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} This concludes the proof. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Bound the distance between A and R
nodes.statement: As a result, for each~$a$, \Cref{lem:trunc-inequality} implies that \begin{equation*} (A_a - R_a)^2 = (A_a - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a))^2 \leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (A_a - (A_a)^2). \end{equation*} Thus, \begin{align*} \sum_a \Vert (A_a - R_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Vert^2 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - R_a)^2 \otimes I\ket{\psi} &\leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a - (A_a)^2) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &\leq \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot 2\zeta. \tag{by \Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}} \end{align*} This implies that $A_a \otimes I \approx_{2\zeta/\delta} R_a \otimes I$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the distance between A and R

nodes.name: Bound R <= (1+2delta)I
nodes.statement: Next, for each $x \in [0, 1]$, it follows from the definition of $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta$ that \begin{equation*} \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot x. \end{equation*} Thus, for each~$a$ \begin{equation*} R_a = \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(A_a) \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot A_a. \end{equation*} Summing over all~$a$, \begin{equation*} R = \sum_a R_a \leq \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot \sum_a A_a = \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot A = \left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\right) \cdot I, \end{equation*} because~$A$ is a measurement. We note that \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{1-\delta} = \frac{1}{1-\delta} \cdot \frac{1 + 2\delta}{1 + 2\delta} = \frac{1 + 2\delta}{1 + \delta - 2\delta^2} \leq 1 + 2\delta, \end{equation*} because \begin{equation*} 1 + \delta - 2\delta^2 = 1 + \delta\cdot(1-2\delta)\geq 1 \end{equation*} when $\delta \leq 1/2$, which we assumed in \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}. Hence, \begin{equation*} R \leq (1+ 2\delta) \cdot I. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Set delta = sqrt(zeta)
nodes.statement: The lemma now follows by setting $\delta = \sqrt{\zeta}$. Note that we required that $\delta$ be at most $1/2$, which follows from our assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}.

nodes.name: Split into two cases
nodes.statement: This is proved by case analysis.

nodes.name: Case x >= 1-delta
nodes.statement: First, suppose that $x \geq 1 - \delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 1$. In addition, because $\delta \leq 1/2$ by \Cref{eq:bound-on-delta}, $ x \geq 1 - \delta \geq 1/2 \geq \delta. $ Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = (1-x)^2\\ &\leq (1-x)\\ &\leq (1-x) \cdot \frac{x}{\delta} \tag{because $x \geq \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Case x < 1-delta
nodes.statement: Next, suppose that $x < 1 -\delta$. This implies that $\mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x) = 0$. Thus, \begin{align*} (x - \mathsf{trunc}_\delta(x))^2 & = x^2\\ &\leq x\\ &\leq x \cdot \frac{(1-x)}{\delta} \tag{because $x \leq 1- \delta$}\\ &= \frac{1}{\delta} \cdot (x - x^2). \end{align*} This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Take R from the rounding lemma and its ranks
nodes.statement: Let $\{R_a\}$ be the set of projective matrices given by \Cref{lem:projective-non-measurement}. For each $a$, let $r_a$ be the rank of $R_a$. Let $r = \sum_a r_a$.
nodes.statement_short: Take R from the rounding lemma and its ranks

nodes.name: Trivial case r <= d; assume r > d
nodes.statement: If $r \leq d$, then the lemma is trivially satisfied by taking $Q$ to be~$R$ and applying \Cref{lem:projective-non-measurement}. Henceforth, we will assume that $r > d$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial case r <= d; assume r > d

nodes.name: r is at most (1+2sqrt(zeta))d
nodes.statement: We want to reduce~$r$ so that it is at most~$d$. Fortunately, it is already not too much larger than~$d$: \begin{equation} r = \sum_{a} r_a = \sum_{a} \mathrm{tr}(R_a) = \mathrm{tr}(R) \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \mathrm{tr}(I) = (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot d. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Orthonormal bases of the ranges
nodes.statement: Let $\ket{v_{a, 1}}, \ldots, \ket{v_{a, r_a}}$ be an orthonormal basis for the range of $R_a$, so that \begin{equation*} R_a = \sum_{i=1}^{r_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Define overlaps and bound total overlap
nodes.statement_short: Define overlaps and bound total overlap

nodes.name: Split into Large and Small sets
nodes.statement: Now we define $\mathsf{Large}$ to be the set of large overlaps: \begin{equation*} \mathsf{Large} = \{(a, i) \mid \text{$o_{a, i}$ is among the~$d$ largest of the $o_{b, j}$'s}\}, \end{equation*} where we break ties arbitrarily, and we define $\mathsf{Small}$ to be the set containing the remaining $(a, i)$'s. We note that $\mathsf{Large}$ is well-defined and has size~$d$ because $r > d$. Hence, \Cref{eq:bound-on-r} implies that \begin{equation} |\mathsf{Small}| = r - |\mathsf{Large}| = r - d \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot d - d = 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot d \leq 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot r. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Split into Large and Small sets

nodes.name: Small overlaps total at most 4sqrt(zeta)
nodes.statement: Thus, the small $(a,i)$'s have small total overlap: \begin{align} \sum_{(a, i) \in \mathsf{Small}} o_{a, i} \leq \frac{|\mathsf{Small}|}{r} \sum_{a, i} o_{a,i} &\leq 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot \sum_{a, i} o_{a,i} \tag{by \Cref{eq:size-of-small-is-small}}\\ &\leq 2\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \tag{by \Cref{eq:total-overlap}}\\ & \leq 4\sqrt{\zeta}, \end{align} where the final step uses the assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}.

nodes.name: Define Q_a and bound its rank
nodes.statement: For each~$a$ we let $\mathsf{Large}_a$ to be set of $i$'s such that $(a,i)$ is contained in $\mathsf{Large}$, and we define $\mathsf{Small}_a$ similarly. We define the matrix \begin{equation*} Q_a = \sum_{i\in \mathsf{Large}_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}. \end{equation*} Then clearly \begin{equation*} \sum_a \mathrm{rank}(Q_a) = \sum_a |\mathsf{Large}_a| = |\mathsf{Large}| \leq d. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define Q_a and bound its rank

nodes.name: Q <= R
nodes.statement: We can compute the difference \begin{equation*} R_a - Q_a = \sum_{i=1}^{r_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}} - \sum_{i \in \mathsf{Large}_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}} = \sum_{i\in \mathsf{Small}_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{v_{a,i}}. \end{equation*} This is a projective Hermitian matrix, which implies that $Q_a \leq R_a$. As a result, \begin{equation*} Q = \sum_a Q_a \leq \sum_a R_a = R \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot I. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: R is close to Q
nodes.statement: In addition, \begin{align*} \sum_a \Vert (R_a - Q_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \Vert^2 &= \sum_a \bra{\psi}(R_a - Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi}(R_a - Q_a)\otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{because $R_a - Q_a$ is a projector}\\ &= \sum_a \sum_{i \in \mathsf{Small}_a} \bra{\psi} \cdot (\ket{v_{a,i}}\bra {v_{a,i}} \otimes I) \cdot\ket{\psi}\\ &= \sum_a \sum_{i \in \mathsf{Small}_a} o_{a, i}\\ &\leq 4\sqrt{\zeta}. \tag{by \Cref{eq:small-overlaps}} \end{align*} This means that \begin{equation*} R_a \otimes I \approx_{4\sqrt{\zeta}} Q_a \otimes I. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Triangle inequality gives A close to Q
nodes.statement: Since we know that $A_a \otimes I \approx_{2\sqrt{\zeta}} R_a \otimes I$ by \Cref{lem:projective-non-measurement}, \Cref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-approx_delta} implies that \begin{equation*} A_a \otimes I \approx_{12\sqrt{\zeta}} Q_a \otimes I. \end{equation*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality gives A close to Q

nodes.name: Replace one Q_a by A_a
nodes.statement: To begin, we claim that \begin{align} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{because the $Q_a$'s are projective}\\ & \approx_{5 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{align} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \otimes I) \cdot ((Q_a - A_a) \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~&\sqrt{\sum_a\bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{1+2\sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot \sqrt{12\sqrt{\zeta}} \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{12\sqrt{\zeta}}, \end{align*} where the last line uses the assumption that $\zeta \leq 1/4$ from \Cref{eq:assumption-on-zeta}.

nodes.name: Replace the other Q_a by A_a
nodes.statement: Next, we claim that \begin{equation} \eqref{eq:Q-for-an-A} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot A_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{4 \zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{align*} &\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((Q_a - A_a) \otimes I) \cdot (A_a \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq~&\sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_a\bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\\ \leq~& \sqrt{12 \sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot 1. \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Replace the other Q_a by A_a

nodes.name: Combine with near-projectivity of A
nodes.statement: In conclusion, \begin{align*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} & \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 9 \zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:Q-for-an-A,eq:another-Q-for-A}}\\ & \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 2\zeta - 9\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:A-looks-projective}}\\ & \geq \bra{\psi} A \otimes I \ket{\psi} - 11 \zeta^{1/4} \nonumber\\ & = 1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Eigendecompose Q and compare sqrt(Q) with Q
nodes.statement_short: Eigendecompose Q and compare sqrt(Q) with Q

nodes.name: Bound the scalar factor by 1-sqrt(zeta)
nodes.statement: We note that \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}}} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta} + \zeta}} = \frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\zeta}} = \frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\zeta}} \cdot \Big(\frac{1-\sqrt{\zeta}}{1-\sqrt{\zeta}}\Big) = \frac{1-\sqrt{\zeta}}{1 - \zeta} \geq 1 - \sqrt{\zeta}. \end{equation*} Hence, $\sqrt{Q} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot Q$.

nodes.name: Apply completeness of Q
nodes.statement: As a result, \Cref{lem:Q-completeness} implies that \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot\bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq (1-\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \left(1 - 11 \zeta^{1/4}\right) \geq 1 -\sqrt{\zeta} - 11 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*} This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Compute X_a^dagger X_a = Q_a
nodes.statement: The first equality follows from \begin{align*} X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a &= \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{a, i} \Big) \cdot \Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, j}}\bra{a, j} \Big)^\dagger\nonumber\\ &= \sum_{i, j=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a, i}}\bra{a, i} \cdot \ket{a, j} \bra{v_{a, j}} = \sum_{i=1}^{m_a} \ket{v_{a,i}}\bra{v_{a,i}} = Q_a. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Use X_a = T_a X and projectivity of T
nodes.statement: The remaining equalities follow from \Cref{lem:xa-t} and the fact that~$T$ is a projective measurement. \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = (X^\dagger \cdot T_a) \cdot (T_a \cdot X) = X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot X = X_a^\dagger \cdot X.\qedhere \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Use X_a = T_a X and projectivity of T

nodes.name: Compute X X^dagger via the SVD
nodes.statement: First, \begin{align*} X \cdot X^\dagger &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute X X^dagger via the SVD

nodes.name: X^dagger X = Q via T a measurement
nodes.statement: Second, \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot X & = \sum_a X^\dagger \cdot T_a X \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ &= \sum_a Q_a \tag{by \Cref{lem:qa-restated}}\\ &= Q. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: X^dagger X = Q via T a measurement

nodes.name: Compute X^dagger X via the SVD
nodes.statement: In addition, we can rewrite $X^\dagger \cdot X$ as \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot X &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\ &= V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger. \end{align*} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Compute X^dagger X via the SVD

nodes.name: Quartic term equals Q_a Q Q_a
nodes.statement: Using~\Cref{lem:X-squared} and~\Cref{lem:qa-restated}, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot Q \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Quartic term equals Q_a Q Q_a

nodes.name: Quadratic term equals Q_a
nodes.statement: Similarly, because $Q_a$ is projective, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a = (X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot (X^\dagger \cdot X_a) = Q_a \cdot Q_a = Q_a. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Identity term equals Q_a
nodes.statement: Finally, \begin{equation*} X_a^\dagger \cdot (I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a = X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Combine the three terms
nodes.statement: Putting these together, \begin{align*} &X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a\\ =~& X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger - 2 \cdot X\cdot X^\dagger + I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a\\ =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - 2 \cdot Q_a + Q_a\\ =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a. \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Compute X X-hat^dagger
nodes.statement: First, \begin{align*} X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\ &= U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Compute X^dagger X-hat = sqrt(Q)
nodes.statement: Second, \begin{align*} X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} &= (U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\ &= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\ &= \sqrt{V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger}\\ &= \sqrt{Q}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}} \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Write the left side as U (Sigma - I)^2 U^dagger
nodes.statement: By~\Cref{lem:X-squared,lem:X-hat-squared,lem:X-times-X-hat}, \begin{align*} (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger & = X \cdot X^\dagger - X\cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger - \widehat{X} \cdot X^\dagger + \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger\\ & = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - 2 \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger+ I_{m \times m}\\ & = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 - 2 \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m} \right) \cdot U^\dagger\\ & = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the left side as U (Sigma - I)^2 U^dagger

nodes.name: Compare (Sigma-I)^2 with (Sigma^2-I)^2
nodes.statement: Because $\Sigma_{m \times m}$ and $I_{m \times m}$ are commuting, \begin{equation*} (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2 \leq (\Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2 = (\Sigma_{m\times m}^2 - I_{m \times m})^2. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Conclude the operator inequality
nodes.statement: As a result, \begin{align*} U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger & \leq U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 - I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger\\ & = \left(U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - I_{m \times m} \right)^2\\ &= (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}} \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Expand the squared distance into four terms
nodes.statement: Our goal is to upper-bound the quantity \begin{align} &\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\ =~& \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \bra{\psi} P\otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}, \end{align} where the last step uses the projectivity of~$Q$ and~$P$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the squared distance into four terms

nodes.name: Bound <Q> by 1+2sqrt(zeta)
nodes.statement: We bound the four terms in \Cref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} separately. First, by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}, \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 1+2\sqrt{\zeta}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name:
Bound

by 1
nodes.statement: Second, because~$P$ is a sub-measurement, \begin{equation*} \bra{\psi} P \otimes I\ket{\psi} \leq 1. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Write cross terms as twice a real part
nodes.statement: The third term and fourth terms are significantly more complicated to bound. As they are complex conjugates of each other, we can write their sum as \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = 2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write cross terms as twice a real part

nodes.name: Rewrite Q_a as X_a^dagger X
nodes.statement: We now focus on the expression on the right-hand side of \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates}. To begin, we use \Cref{lem:qa-restated} to rewrite it as \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Exchange X for X-hat via Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: The main step will be to show that we can exchange the second $X$ for an $\widehat{X}$, i.e. \begin{equation} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}. \end{equation} To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference. \begin{multline*} \Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X})) \otimes I) \cdot(P_a \otimes I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\ \leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}}\cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}}. \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Exchange X for X-hat via Cauchy-Schwarz

nodes.name: Bound the first factor by 4sqrt(zeta)
nodes.statement: The expression inside the first square root is \begin{align*} & \sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ \leq~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:squared-difference}}\\ =~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}}\\ \leq~& 4\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by~\Cref{lem:q-almost-projective}}\\ =~& 4\sqrt{\zeta}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Second factor at most 1
nodes.statement: The expression inside the second square root is at most~$1$ because~$P$ is a sub-measurement.

nodes.name: The exchanged expression equals <sqrt(Q)>
nodes.statement: Next, we claim that the \Cref{eq:add-a-hat} is in fact a real-valued expression. To see this, \begin{align*} \eqref{eq:add-a-hat} & = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:xa-t,lem:pa-restated}}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\ &= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\ &= \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}) \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\ &= \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-times-X-hat}}, \end{align*} which is real-valued because~$Q$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Lower bound via completeness of sqrt(Q)
nodes.statement: As a result, we have \begin{align*} \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) & \geq \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) - 2\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:add-a-hat}}\\ & = \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \otimes I \ket{\psi}- 2\zeta^{1/4}\\ & \geq (1 - 12 \zeta^{1/4}) - 2\zeta^{1/4}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:sqrt-Q-completeness}} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound via completeness of sqrt(Q)

nodes.name: Cross terms at least 2(1-14zeta^{1/4})
nodes.statement: In total, \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates} shows that \begin{equation*} \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} \geq 2 \cdot(1 - 14\zeta^{1/4}). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Combine to 30zeta^{1/4}
nodes.statement: Putting everything together, we conclude that \begin{equation*} \eqref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} \leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) + 1 - 2\cdot (1-14\zeta^{1/4}) = 2\sqrt{\zeta} + 28 \zeta^{1/4} \leq 30 \zeta^{1/4}. \end{equation*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Fix the original (non-symmetric) strategy
nodes.statement: Suppose $(\psi, A^{\mathrm{A}},B^{\mathrm{A}},L^{\mathrm{A}},A^{\mathrm{B}},B^{\mathrm{B}},L^{\mathrm{B}})$ is a (not necessarily symmetric) strategy which passes the $(m, q, d)$-low individual degree test with probability $(1-\epsilon)$. Throughout this proof we will refer to this as the \emph{original strategy}.

nodes.name: The strategy is (3eps,3eps,3eps)-good
nodes.statement: Then because each of the three subtests occurs with probability $1/3$, $(\psi, A^{\mathrm{A}},B^{\mathrm{A}},L^{\mathrm{A}},A^{\mathrm{B}},B^{\mathrm{B}},L^{\mathrm{B}})$ is a $(3\epsilon, 3\epsilon, 3\epsilon)$-good strategy.

nodes.name: Plan: symmetrize, apply induction, unsymmetrize
nodes.statement: We now would like to apply \Cref{thm:main-induction}, but it only applies to strategies which are symmetric. So we will apply a standard construction to ``symmetrize'' our strategy, apply \Cref{thm:main-induction}, and then ``unsymmetrize'' the resulting $\{G_g\}$ measurement to obtain $\{G^{\mathrm{A}}_g\}$ and $\{G^{\mathrm{B}}_g\}$ measurements.

nodes.name: WLOG equal local dimensions
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we will assume that Player~$\mathrm{A}$ and~$\mathrm{B}$'s Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{B}}$ are both $\mathbb C^d$, for some~$d$. (This argument can be extended to the case of different dimensions in a straightforward manner.)

nodes.name: Define the symmetrized state with role registers
nodes.statement: We will introduce two additional registers, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}'} =\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{B'}} = \mathbb C^2$, referred to as the \emph{role registers}. Then the symmetrized state is given by \begin{equation*} \ket{\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}} = \ket{0}_{\mathrm{A}'}\ket{1}_{\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\psi}_{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}} +\ket{1}_{\mathrm{A}'}\ket{0}_{\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\psi_{\mathrm{swap}}}_{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}} \in (\mathbb C^2_{\mathrm{A}'} \otimes \mathbb C^d_{\mathrm{A}}) \otimes (\mathbb C^2_{\mathrm{B}'} \otimes \mathbb C^d_{\mathrm{B}}), \end{equation*} where $\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{swap}}}$ denotes $\ket{\psi}$ with its two registers swapped. Note that the resulting state $\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}}$ is symmetric under the exchange of its two registers.
nodes.statement_short: Define the symmetrized state with role registers

nodes.name: Define symmetrized measurements
nodes.statement: Next, we define the symmetrized measurement $A_{\mathrm{sym}} = \{(A_{\mathrm{sym}})^u_a\}$ as follows \begin{equation*} (A_{\mathrm{sym}})^u_a = \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes A^{\mathrm{A},u}_a + \ket{1} \bra{1} \otimes A^{\mathrm{B},u}_a, \end{equation*} and we define $B_{\mathrm{sym}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ similarly.

nodes.name: The symmetrized strategy is symmetric and good
nodes.statement: The strategy $(\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}, A_{\mathrm{sym}}, B_{\mathrm{sym}}, L_{\mathrm{sym}})$ is symmetric; we refer to it as the \emph{symmetrized strategy}. It has the following interpretation: the two players measure their respective role registers in the standard basis; the one that receives a ``$0$'' will act as Player~A in the original strategy, and the one that receives a ``$1$'' will act as Player~B in the original strategy. As a result, the symmetrized strategy is also a $(3\epsilon, 3\epsilon, 3\epsilon)$-good strategy.
nodes.statement_short: The symmetrized strategy is symmetric and good

nodes.name: Apply the main induction to get G
nodes.statement: Now we apply \cref{thm:main-induction} to the symmetrized strategy. To do so, set \begin{align*} &1000k^2 m^2 \cdot\Big((3\epsilon)^{1/1024} + (3\epsilon)^{1/1024} + (3\epsilon)^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big)\\ \leq{}& 10000 k^2 m^2 \cdot \Big(\epsilon^{1/1024} + (d/q)^{1/1024}\Big) =: \nu, \end{align*} and set $\sigma = m^2\cdot\left(\nu + e^{-k/(80000m^2)}\right)$. Then \Cref{thm:main-induction} produces a measurement $G = \{G_g\} \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ such that \begin{equation} (A_{\mathrm{sym}})^{u}_a \otimes I \simeq_{\sigma} I \otimes G_{[g(u)=a]}, \quad \text{and} \quad G_{[g(u)=a]} \otimes I \simeq_{\sigma} I \otimes (A_{\mathrm{sym}})^u_a. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the main induction to get G

nodes.name: Define G^A and G^B by projecting role registers
nodes.statement: Now we unsymmetrize the symmetrized strategy to derive measurements $\{G^w_g\}$ for $w \in \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\}$. Letting $I_d$ denote the $d \times d$ identity operator, define the operators \begin{gather*} G^{\mathrm{A}}_g = (\bra{0} \otimes I_d) \cdot G_g\cdot (\ket{0} \otimes I_d) \\ G^{\mathrm{B}}_g = (\bra{1} \otimes I_d) \cdot G_g\cdot (\ket{1} \otimes I_d), \end{gather*} where $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$ act on the $\mathbb C^2$ part of $G_g$. Thus, $G^{\mathrm{A}}_g, G^{\mathrm{B}}_g$ are positive operators acting on $\mathbb C^d$, and furthermore they form POVMs: \[ \sum_g G^{\mathrm{A}}_g = \sum_g (\bra{0} \otimes I_d) \cdot G_g \cdot (\ket{0} \otimes I_d) = (\bra{0} \otimes I_d) \cdot \Big(\sum_g G_g\Big) \cdot (\ket{0} \otimes I_d) = I_d\;. \] The same derivation holds for $G^{\mathrm{B}}_g$.

nodes.statement: We have now derived everything we wanted, except that~$G$ is not necessarily projective. To remedy this, we apply the orthogonalization lemma for measurements (\Cref{lem:orthonormalization-main-lemma}) to \Cref{eq:G-self-consistency}. It implies the existence of two projective sub-measurements $P^{\mathrm{A}} = \{P^{\mathrm{A}}\}, P^{\mathrm{B}} = \{P^{\mathrm{B}}\} \in \polysub{m}{q}{d}$ such that \begin{align*} G^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I &\approx_{100\zeta_1^{1/4}} P^{\mathrm{A}}_g \otimes I,\\ I \otimes G^{\mathrm{B}}_g &\approx_{100\zeta_1^{1/4}} I \otimes P^{\mathrm{B}}_g. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Conclude the three bounds
nodes.statement: Hence, \Cref{eq:one-goal,eq:another-goal,eq:third-goal} provide the three bounds we want. This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Self-consistency test
nodes.statement: We begin with the self-consistency test. Here, both provers are given a uniformly random point $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}})$, they measure using $A^{\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}} = (A^{{\boldsymbol{x}}})^{\boldsymbol{u}}$, and they succeed if their outcomes are the same. This is equivalent to performing the self-consistency test on the ${\boldsymbol{x}}$-restricted strategy, averaged over ${\boldsymbol{x}}$, and so $\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \delta_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \leq \delta$. (It is a ``$\leq$" rather than an ``$=$" because $\delta$ is just an upper-bound on the failure probability.)

nodes.name: Axis-parallel lines test
nodes.statement: Next, we consider the axis-parallel lines test. Suppose the provers are sent the line $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ and the point $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}) \in \boldsymbol{\ell}$. With probability $\frac{1}{m+1}$, $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is parallel to the $(m+1)$-st direction. When it is not, then $\boldsymbol{\ell} = \mathrm{append}_x(\boldsymbol{\ell}')$, where $\boldsymbol{\ell}'$ is an axis-parallel line in $\mathbb F_q^m$. In this case, the points prover measures with the measurement $A^{\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}} = (A^{\boldsymbol{x}})^{\boldsymbol{u}}$ and receives an outcome $\boldsymbol{a}$, the lines prover measures with the measurement $B^{\boldsymbol{\ell}} = (B^{{\boldsymbol{x}}})^{\boldsymbol{\ell}'}$ and receives an outcome $\boldsymbol{f} = \mathrm{append}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}(\boldsymbol{f}')$, and they succeed if $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}) = \boldsymbol{a}$, or, equivalently, if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{a}$. Hence, the probability that they succeed is equal to the probability that the ${\boldsymbol{x}}$-restricted strategy passes the $(m, q, d)$-low individual degree test, which is $\epsilon_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}$. As a result, \begin{align*} \epsilon &\geq \mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}, \boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}}[\text{$A$ and $B$ succeed given $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}})$}]\\ &\geq \left(\frac{m}{m+1}\right) \cdot \mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\boldsymbol{\ell}, \boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}}}[\text{$A$ and $B$ succeed given $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, $(\boldsymbol{u}, {\boldsymbol{x}})$} \mid \text{$\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is not parallel to direction $m+1$}]\\ & = \left(\frac{m}{m+1}\right) \cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}} \epsilon_{{\boldsymbol{x}}}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Diagonal lines test is analogous
nodes.statement: Finally, the analysis of the diagonal lines test follows the same proof as the axis-parallel lines test, and we omit it here.

nodes.name: WLOG all parameters at most 1
nodes.statement: We note that the bound we are proving is trivial when at least one of $\epsilon$, $\delta$, $\gamma$, or $d/q$ is $\geq 1$, as $\nu$ is at least~$1$ in that case. Hence, we may assume that $\epsilon, \delta, \gamma, d/q \leq 1$. This will aid us when carrying out the error calculations, as it allows us to bound terms like $(d/q)^{1/2}$ by terms like $(d/q)^{1/4}$.

nodes.name: Base case m = 1 from the lines measurement
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on~$m$. The base case is when $m = 1$. In this case, there is only one axis-parallel line~$\ell$ in $\mathbb F_q^m$, and so $B^\ell \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$. Because this strategy fails the axis-parallel line test with probability at most~$\epsilon$, \begin{equation*} A^u_a \otimes I \simeq_{\epsilon} I \otimes B^\ell_{[f(u) = a]}, \end{equation*} on average over $\boldsymbol{u} \sim \mathbb F_q$. We note that this bound holds independent of the value of~$k$. This is even better than the theorem demands, and so the theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Base case m = 1 from the lines measurement
